document.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act)

articles.heading: Subject Matter
articles.summary: Article 1 of the EU AI Act — Subject Matter. Sets the Regulation's purpose: improve the internal market while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety, fundamental rights, democracy, the rule of law and the environment against harmful effects of AI, and support innovation. Article 1(2) enumerates the seven pillars the Regulation lays down: harmonised market rules for AI systems, prohibitions, high-risk requirements and operator obligations, transparency rules, GPAI model rules, market surveillance and governance, and innovation-support measures including for SMEs. Route here for questions about the Regulation's objectives, framing, or which pillar a topic falls under.

articles.heading: Scope
articles.summary: Article 2 of the EU AI Act — Scope. The territorial and material reach of the Regulation, including the extraterritorial hook in Art 2(1)(c) that catches non-EU providers and deployers when AI output is used in the Union. Carves out major exclusions: national security, military and defence (2(3)), public authorities of third countries acting under cooperation agreements (2(4)), scientific research and development (2(6)), pre-market testing (2(8)), and personal non-professional use (2(10)). Also addresses interplay with sectoral law and free and open-source AI. Route here for any 'does the AI Act apply to X?' question.

articles.heading: Definitions
articles.summary: Article 3 of the EU AI Act — Definitions. The interpretive dictionary: 68 numbered definitions including 'AI system' (3(1) aligned to OECD), 'provider', 'deployer', 'importer', 'distributor', 'operator', 'placing on the market', 'putting into service', 'general-purpose AI model', 'general-purpose AI system', 'systemic risk', 'high-risk AI system', 'safety component', 'biometric data', 'emotion recognition', 'remote biometric identification', 'critical infrastructure', 'serious incident' and 'substantial modification'. The first stop for any question about whether an actor or artefact falls within a defined category.

articles.heading: AI literacy

paragraphs.summary: Article 4(1) of the EU AI Act — AI literacy obligation. Both providers and deployers of any AI system (not just high-risk) must take measures to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among staff and other persons who operate or use the AI system on their behalf. Measures must account for the persons' technical knowledge, experience, education, training, and the context the system is used in, as well as the affected persons. One of the few horizontal duties that bites from 2 February 2025 across the entire AI value chain regardless of risk tier.

articles.summary: Article 4 of the EU AI Act — AI literacy. Horizontal duty: providers and deployers must take measures to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level of AI literacy among their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf, taking into account technical knowledge, experience, education, training and the context the systems are used in and the persons or groups affected. Applies to all AI systems in scope, not only high-risk. Applies from 2 February 2025 — the first substantive obligation to bite. MVP-critical (sub-paragraphs handled separately).

articles.heading: Prohibited AI Practices
articles.summary: Article 5 of the EU AI Act — Prohibited AI Practices. The 'red line' catalogue. Bans placing on the market, putting into service or using AI systems that deploy subliminal/manipulative or exploitative techniques causing significant harm; social scoring by public or private actors; predictive policing based solely on profiling; untargeted scraping for facial recognition databases; emotion inference in workplace and education (with narrow medical/safety carve-outs); biometric categorisation inferring sensitive attributes; and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces by law enforcement (with strict authorised exceptions in 5(2)–(7)). Applies from 2 February 2025.

articles.heading: Classification Rules for High-Risk AI Systems

paragraphs.summary: Article 6(1) of the EU AI Act — high-risk classification, product-bound track (chapeau). Sets the two cumulative conditions under which an AI system qualifies as high-risk because it is tied to a regulated product, irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of that product. Both points (a) and (b) must be satisfied. This is the gateway for the Annex I 'product-safety' route to high-risk status, complementing the standalone Annex III route in paragraph 2.

paragraphs.label: 1(a)
paragraphs.summary: Article 6(1)(a) of the EU AI Act — high-risk classification by Annex I product safety. First condition of the product-bound prong: the AI system must either be used as a safety component of a product, or itself be a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I (machinery, toys, lifts, medical devices, in-vitro diagnostics, civil aviation, motor vehicles, marine equipment, etc.). Used together with Article 6(1)(b) to scope the product-bound high-risk track.

paragraphs.label: 1(b)
paragraphs.summary: Article 6(1)(b) of the EU AI Act — high-risk classification triggered by third-party conformity assessment. Second cumulative condition of the product-bound prong: the host product (or the AI-system-as-product) must be required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment for placing on the market or putting into service under the relevant Annex I sectoral legislation. Where only self-assessment is permitted under the sectoral act, the AI system is not high-risk via this route.

Article 6(2) of the EU AI Act — standalone high-risk classification via Annex III. In addition to the product-bound systems under paragraph 1, any AI system whose intended purpose falls within the eight use-case areas of Annex III (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, access to essential services, law enforcement, migration/border control, administration of justice and democratic processes) is high-risk. This is the dynamic list the Commission may amend by delegated act under Article 7.

Article 6(3) of the EU AI Act — derogation from Annex III high-risk status (chapeau). An Annex III AI system is not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing decision-making outcomes. The derogation applies where one or more of the four cumulative conditions in (a)–(d) is met, but never where the system performs profiling of natural persons (which always remains high-risk).

paragraphs.label: 3(a)
paragraphs.summary: Article 6(3)(a) of the EU AI Act — narrow procedural task carve-out. First trigger condition for the Annex III derogation: the AI system is intended to perform a narrow procedural task. Captures lightweight workflow helpers such as classification, routing, or templating that don't materially influence the underlying decision. Read together with the chapeau in Article 6(3), which still requires no significant risk and no profiling of natural persons.

paragraphs.label: 3(b)
paragraphs.summary: Article 6(3)(b) of the EU AI Act — improving a completed human activity. Second derogation trigger: the AI system is intended to improve the result of a previously completed human activity (for example, polishing or formatting a draft already produced by a human). The human assessment remains the authoritative output. Subject to the chapeau gate that the system must not pose significant risk and must not profile natural persons.

paragraphs.label: 3(c)
paragraphs.summary: Article 6(3)(c) of the EU AI Act — pattern detection without replacing human assessment. Third derogation trigger: the AI system is intended to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review. Targets analytic / monitoring tools that flag anomalies for a human to consider rather than acting on them autonomously.

paragraphs.label: 3(d)
paragraphs.summary: Article 6(3)(d) of the EU AI Act — preparatory task carve-out. Fourth derogation trigger: the AI system is intended to perform a preparatory task to an assessment relevant for the Annex III use cases (e.g. file indexing, translation, transcription that feeds into a downstream high-risk decision but does not itself decide). Subject to the Article 6(3) chapeau and the absolute bar on profiling natural persons.

Article 6(4) of the EU AI Act — documentation duty for providers self-classifying out. A provider that concludes its Annex III system is not high-risk under the paragraph 3 derogation must document that assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service, and must register under Article 49(2). On reasoned request, national competent authorities can require the documentation. Misclassification exposes the provider to enforcement and fines.

Article 6(5) of the EU AI Act — Commission guidelines on Article 6. Mandates the Commission, after consulting the AI Board, to issue by 2 February 2026 guidelines under Article 96 specifying the practical implementation of Article 6, including a comprehensive list of practical examples of use cases on the high-risk / non-high-risk borderline. Operational anchor for stakeholders' classification decisions and for supervisory authorities reviewing them.

Article 6(6) of the EU AI Act — delegated power to add or tighten derogation conditions. Empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts under Article 97 to amend the conditions in Article 6(3) by adding new ones or modifying existing ones, where there is concrete and reliable evidence that AI systems falling within Annex III but not posing significant risk exist. Mechanism to keep the high-risk gateway calibrated as evidence accumulates.

Article 6(7) of the EU AI Act — mandatory deletion of derogation conditions when evidence requires. Obliges the Commission to adopt delegated acts under Article 97 deleting any of the Article 6(3) derogation conditions where there is concrete and reliable evidence that doing so is necessary to maintain the level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights provided by the Regulation. Counterweight to paragraph 6's expansion power.

Article 6(8) of the EU AI Act — non-regression and consistency safeguard. Any amendment to the derogation conditions under paragraphs 6 or 7 must not decrease the overall level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights provided by the Regulation, and must ensure consistency with delegated acts adopted under Article 7(1) (Annex III amendments). Locks in a ratchet against weakening the high-risk gateway via delegated acts.

articles.summary: Article 6 of the EU AI Act — Classification rules for high-risk AI systems. The decisional gateway: an AI system is high-risk either because it is a safety component of (or itself) a product covered by Annex I Union harmonisation law that requires third-party conformity assessment (Art 6(1)), or because it is listed in an Annex III use case (Art 6(2)). Art 6(3) carves out a 'not high-risk' derogation when an Annex III system performs only narrow procedural tasks, improves prior human activity, detects decision-making patterns, or does preparatory work — but profiling of natural persons always remains high-risk. Determines whether Chapter III obligations (Arts 8–17) attach. Applies from 2 August 2026. MVP-critical.

articles.heading: Amendments to Annex III
articles.summary: Article 7 of the EU AI Act — Amendments to Annex III. Empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts adding, modifying or removing high-risk use cases in Annex III, subject to criteria including the intended purpose, the extent of use, the nature and quantity of data processed, the degree of autonomy, prior incidents, the severity and scale of harm, the irreversibility of outcomes, the vulnerability of affected persons, and the availability of effective redress. The legal hook for keeping the high-risk list living.

articles.heading: Compliance with the Requirements
articles.summary: Article 8 of the EU AI Act — Compliance with the Requirements. Umbrella clause: high-risk AI systems must comply with the requirements of Chapter III Section 2 (Arts 9–15), taking their intended purpose and the generally acknowledged state of the art into account. When sectoral Union law (e.g., medical devices, machinery) already imposes overlapping requirements, providers may integrate AI Act compliance into existing processes to avoid duplication. Establishes the duty to satisfy each downstream requirement and the principle of integrated compliance.

articles.heading: Risk Management System

paragraphs.summary: Article 9(1) of the EU AI Act — duty to establish a risk management system. Providers of high-risk AI systems must establish, implement, document and maintain a risk management system. The four verbs are cumulative — paper-only programmes do not satisfy the requirement. Anchors the rest of Article 9 (lifecycle process, identification, evaluation, residual-risk acceptability, testing) and the first concrete obligation in the Section 2 high-risk requirement set.

Article 9(2) of the EU AI Act — continuous-lifecycle risk management process (chapeau). The risk management system must be a continuous, iterative process planned and run across the entire lifecycle of the high-risk AI system, with regular systematic review and updating. Introduces the four-step process detailed in points (a)–(d): identification, estimation/evaluation, post-market evidence, and adoption of mitigation measures.

paragraphs.label: 2(a)
paragraphs.summary: Article 9(2)(a) of the EU AI Act — risk identification step. The provider must identify and analyse the known and reasonably foreseeable risks the high-risk AI system can pose to health, safety or fundamental rights when used in accordance with its intended purpose. First of the four mandatory steps in the lifecycle risk-management process, scoping the universe of risks to be evaluated and mitigated in points (b)–(d).

paragraphs.label: 2(b)
paragraphs.summary: Article 9(2)(b) of the EU AI Act — risk estimation and evaluation, including foreseeable misuse. Second step: estimate and evaluate risks that may emerge from use in accordance with the intended purpose and under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse. Explicit inclusion of foreseeable misuse forces providers to model adversarial or off-label deployment, not only nominal usage.

paragraphs.label: 2(c)
paragraphs.summary: Article 9(2)(c) of the EU AI Act — feedback from post-market monitoring. Third step: evaluate other risks possibly arising on the basis of data gathered from the post-market monitoring system required under Article 72. Closes the loop between in-field evidence and pre-market design assumptions, ensuring the risk picture is updated when reality diverges from the original safety case.

paragraphs.label: 2(d)
paragraphs.summary: Article 9(2)(d) of the EU AI Act — adoption of risk management measures. Fourth step: adopt appropriate and targeted risk management measures designed to address the risks identified under point (a). Together with paragraph 5's hierarchy (eliminate, mitigate, inform) this is where identified risks must be operationalised into design, controls and information for deployers.

Article 9(3) of the EU AI Act — scope of risks addressed under Article 9. The risks under Article 9 are only those that can be reasonably mitigated or eliminated through the development or design of the high-risk AI system, or through the provision of adequate technical information. Limits Article 9's reach to risks the provider can act on, deliberately leaving deployer-side organisational risks to other provisions (Article 14 oversight, Article 26 deployer duties).

Article 9(4) of the EU AI Act — interaction with other Section 2 requirements. Risk management measures under paragraph 2(d) must give due consideration to the combined effects and possible interactions arising from applying the other Section 2 requirements (data, documentation, logging, transparency, oversight, accuracy/robustness). Forces the provider to view the requirement set holistically rather than satisfying each in isolation.

Article 9(5) of the EU AI Act — residual-risk acceptability and hierarchy of measures (chapeau). Risk management measures must drive each hazard's residual risk, and the overall residual risk of the high-risk AI system, to a level judged acceptable. In identifying the most appropriate measures the provider must follow the hierarchy laid down in points (a)–(c): eliminate by design, then control, then inform/train deployers.

paragraphs.label: 5(a)
paragraphs.summary: Article 9(5)(a) of the EU AI Act — eliminate or reduce by design. First level of the risk-mitigation hierarchy: eliminate or reduce risks identified and evaluated under Article 9(2), as far as technically feasible, through adequate design and development of the high-risk AI system. Design-out always takes precedence over downstream controls or warnings.

paragraphs.label: 5(b)
paragraphs.summary: Article 9(5)(b) of the EU AI Act — mitigation and control measures for residual risks. Second level of the hierarchy: where appropriate, implement adequate mitigation and control measures addressing risks that cannot be eliminated by design. Captures guardrails, output filters, rate limits, and other safeguards layered on top of the base system.

paragraphs.label: 5(c)
paragraphs.summary: Article 9(5)(c) of the EU AI Act — information and training to deployers. Third level of the hierarchy: provide the information required under Article 13 and, where appropriate, training to deployers so that residual risks tied to use can be reduced. Due regard must be given to the deployer's expected technical knowledge, education and training, and the context of deployment.

Article 9(6) of the EU AI Act — duty to test high-risk AI systems. High-risk AI systems must be tested to identify the most appropriate and targeted risk management measures. Testing must ensure they perform consistently for their intended purpose and comply with the Section 2 requirements. Establishes testing as the empirical evidence base for the rest of the Article 9 process.

Article 9(7) of the EU AI Act — testing in real-world conditions permitted. Testing procedures may include testing in real-world conditions in accordance with Article 60 (which sets the conditions, safeguards and oversight for real-world testing outside regulatory sandboxes). Opens the door to operational testing while routing it through Article 60's procedural guardrails.

Article 9(8) of the EU AI Act — timing and methodology of testing. Testing must be performed as appropriate throughout development and, in any event, prior to placing on the market or putting into service. It must be carried out against prior-defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds appropriate to the intended purpose. Forces objective acceptance criteria fixed in advance rather than post-hoc rationalisation of results.

Article 9(9) of the EU AI Act — vulnerable groups, including minors. When implementing the risk management system, providers must consider whether the high-risk AI system, given its intended purpose, is likely to have an adverse impact on persons under 18 and, as appropriate, on other vulnerable groups. Embeds an explicit vulnerability lens into the Article 9 process.

Article 9(10) of the EU AI Act — integration with sectoral risk management. For providers already subject to internal risk-management requirements under other Union law (e.g. medical devices, financial services), the aspects in Article 9(1)–(9) may be part of, or combined with, the risk management procedures established under that law. Avoids duplicative parallel regimes for regulated providers.

articles.summary: Article 9 of the EU AI Act — Risk Management System. Providers of high-risk AI systems must establish, implement, document and maintain a continuous, iterative risk management system across the entire lifecycle. Steps: identify and analyse known and reasonably foreseeable risks (including to health, safety and fundamental rights), estimate residual risks, evaluate post-market data, and adopt targeted mitigation. Risk control measures must aim at elimination or reduction through design, adequate mitigation, and information/training for deployers. Special attention to children and other vulnerable groups. Applies from 2 August 2026. MVP-critical.

articles.heading: Data and Data Governance

paragraphs.summary: Article 10(1) of the EU AI Act — data quality gate for trained high-risk AI systems. High-risk AI systems that involve training of AI models with data must be developed on the basis of training, validation and testing data sets that meet the quality criteria in Article 10(2)–(5), whenever such data sets are used. Anchors the data-governance regime that applies upstream of placing the system on the market.

Article 10(2) of the EU AI Act — data governance and management practices (chapeau). Training, validation and testing data sets must be subject to data governance and management practices appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system. Points (a)–(h) enumerate the specific practices: design choices, collection origin, preparation, assumptions, suitability, bias examination, bias mitigation, and gap identification.

paragraphs.label: 2(a)
paragraphs.summary: Article 10(2)(a) of the EU AI Act — data-governance practice: design choices. Data governance must cover the relevant design choices made in the data lifecycle (which target variable, which features, what labelling schema, what splits). First of the eight enumerated data-governance practices under Article 10(2).

paragraphs.label: 2(b)
paragraphs.summary: Article 10(2)(b) of the EU AI Act — data collection processes and origin, including GDPR purpose. Data governance must cover data collection processes and the origin of the data and, in the case of personal data, the original purpose for which the personal data were collected. Intersects directly with GDPR Article 5(1)(b) purpose limitation: secondary use for training requires a compatibility analysis.

paragraphs.label: 2(c)
paragraphs.summary: Article 10(2)(c) of the EU AI Act — data preparation operations. Data governance must cover relevant data preparation processing operations such as annotation, labelling, cleaning, updating, enrichment and aggregation. Captures the full preprocessing pipeline that turns raw collected data into model inputs.

paragraphs.label: 2(d)
paragraphs.summary: Article 10(2)(d) of the EU AI Act — formulation of assumptions about the data. Data governance must cover the formulation of assumptions, in particular what the data is supposed to measure and represent. Forces documentation of the construct-validity assumptions that justify treating the data as a proxy for the real-world phenomenon.

paragraphs.label: 2(e)
paragraphs.summary: Article 10(2)(e) of the EU AI Act — assessment of data availability and suitability. Data governance must cover an assessment of the availability, quantity and suitability of the data sets that are needed for the intended purpose. Triggers an explicit gap analysis between what is available and what the use case requires.

paragraphs.label: 2(f)
paragraphs.summary: Article 10(2)(f) of the EU AI Act — examination for biases harming rights or safety. Data governance must include examination in view of possible biases likely to affect health and safety, negatively impact fundamental rights, or lead to discrimination prohibited under Union law, particularly where data outputs feed back into inputs for future operations. Targets feedback-loop amplification as well as static bias.

paragraphs.label: 2(g)
paragraphs.summary: Article 10(2)(g) of the EU AI Act — measures to detect, prevent and mitigate biases. Data governance must include appropriate measures to detect, prevent and mitigate possible biases identified under point (f). Pairs with paragraph 5's narrow special-categories carve-out enabling processing of sensitive data strictly necessary for bias correction.

paragraphs.label: 2(h)
paragraphs.summary: Article 10(2)(h) of the EU AI Act — identification of data gaps and shortcomings. Data governance must identify relevant data gaps or shortcomings that prevent compliance with the Regulation and how they can be addressed. Closes the loop with point (e): an evidenced gap analysis with remediation plans, not just narrative.

Article 10(3) of the EU AI Act — data quality criteria. Training, validation and testing data sets must be relevant, sufficiently representative, and — to the best extent possible — free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose. They must have appropriate statistical properties, including with respect to the persons or groups on whom the system is intended to be used. Core dataset-quality obligation rather than a process step.

Article 10(4) of the EU AI Act — geographic, contextual, behavioural and functional specificity. Data sets must take into account, to the extent required by the intended purpose, the characteristics or elements particular to the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural or functional setting in which the high-risk AI system is intended to be used. Locks dataset fitness to the deployment context, not a generic 'world average'.

Article 10(5) of the EU AI Act — special-category processing for bias correction (chapeau). To the extent strictly necessary for bias detection and correction under Article 10(2)(f)–(g), providers may exceptionally process special categories of personal data (GDPR Article 9). This is the explicit derogation that aligns with GDPR. The processing is conditional on cumulative safeguards listed in points (a)–(f).

paragraphs.label: 5(a)
paragraphs.summary: Article 10(5)(a) of the EU AI Act — necessity test for special-categories use. First cumulative safeguard for the Article 10(5) bias-correction carve-out: the provider must demonstrate that bias detection and correction could not be effectively achieved using alternative data such as synthetic or anonymised data. Establishes a last-resort test before sensitive-data processing is permissible.

paragraphs.label: 5(b)
paragraphs.summary: Article 10(5)(b) of the EU AI Act — technical limitations and state-of-the-art protection. Second safeguard: the special categories of personal data must be subject to technical limitations on the re-use of the personal data, and to state-of-the-art security and privacy-preserving measures, including pseudonymisation. Calibrates the safeguard expectation against current state of the art.

paragraphs.label: 5(c)
paragraphs.summary: Article 10(5)(c) of the EU AI Act — access controls and documentation. Third safeguard: the special categories of personal data must be subject to measures ensuring the data are secured, protected and subject to suitable safeguards, including strict controls and documentation of access to avoid misuse and ensure only authorised persons have access.

paragraphs.label: 5(d)
paragraphs.summary: Article 10(5)(d) of the EU AI Act — no onward transfer. Fourth safeguard: the special categories of personal data must not be transmitted, transferred or otherwise accessed by other parties. Hard prohibition on data egress beyond the provider's bias-correction perimeter.

paragraphs.label: 5(e)
paragraphs.summary: Article 10(5)(e) of the EU AI Act — deletion duty. Fifth safeguard: the special categories of personal data must be deleted once the bias has been corrected or the retention period has been reached, whichever comes first. Pairs the necessity test in (a) with a hard end-of-life requirement.

paragraphs.label: 5(f)
paragraphs.summary: Article 10(5)(f) of the EU AI Act — records of processing activities. Sixth safeguard: the records of processing activities under GDPR (Regulation 2016/679), Regulation 2018/1725 and Directive 2016/680 must include the reasons why processing special categories was strictly necessary to detect and correct biases, and why that objective could not be achieved by processing other data. Pushes the necessity justification into the auditable RoPA.

Article 10(6) of the EU AI Act — non-trained high-risk AI systems. For high-risk AI systems that do not use techniques involving the training of AI models, paragraphs 2 to 5 apply only to the testing data sets. Narrows the Article 10 burden for rule-based or otherwise non-trained systems to the data used to validate performance.

articles.summary: Article 10 of the EU AI Act — Data and Data Governance. Where high-risk AI systems use techniques that involve training models with data, training, validation and testing datasets must meet quality criteria: appropriate governance practices covering design choices, collection processes, data preparation operations, relevance, representativeness, error checks, and examination of biases that could affect health, safety or fundamental rights or lead to prohibited discrimination. Datasets must be sufficiently complete, free of errors and statistically appropriate to the intended purpose. Article 10(5) creates a narrow legal basis to process special-category personal data strictly for bias detection and correction. Applies from 2 August 2026. MVP-critical.

articles.heading: Technical Documentation

paragraphs.summary: Article 11(1) of the EU AI Act — technical documentation duty. Technical documentation for a high-risk AI system must be drawn up before placement on the market or putting into service, kept up to date, and structured to demonstrate compliance with Section 2 and to give competent authorities and notified bodies the information needed to assess conformity. Contents must include at least the elements set out in Annex IV. The foundational artefact for conformity assessment and supervisory engagement.

Article 11(2) of the EU AI Act — integration with sectoral product documentation. Where a high-risk AI system relates to a product covered by Section A of Annex I (e.g. machinery, lifts, medical devices), a single set of technical documentation must be drawn up containing both the AI Act information in paragraph 1 and the information required under the relevant Annex I act. Avoids parallel files for the same product.

Article 11(3) of the EU AI Act — Commission power to amend Annex IV. Empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts under Article 97 to amend Annex IV where necessary, so that the technical documentation continues to provide all information needed to assess compliance in light of technical progress. Keeps the documentation requirements current as AI techniques evolve.

articles.summary: Article 11 of the EU AI Act — Technical Documentation. Providers of high-risk AI systems must draw up technical documentation before the system is placed on the market and keep it up to date. Documentation must demonstrate compliance with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements and provide market surveillance authorities with the information needed to assess conformity. Annex IV sets the mandatory contents (general description, design, data, monitoring, performance, risk management). SMEs and startups may use a simplified template provided by the Commission (11(1) second subparagraph). Applies from 2 August 2026. MVP-critical.

articles.heading: Record-Keeping

paragraphs.summary: Article 12(1) of the EU AI Act — automatic event logging duty. High-risk AI systems must technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system. The obligation is on the design itself — providers must build logging in; the deployer-side retention duty sits in Article 26(6).

Article 12(2) of the EU AI Act — purposes of logging (chapeau). To ensure traceability appropriate to the intended purpose, logging capabilities must enable the recording of events relevant to the purposes listed in points (a)–(c): risk/substantial-modification detection, post-market monitoring, and monitoring of operation by deployers under Article 26(5). Defines the minimum functional scope of the logging design.

paragraphs.label: 2(a)
paragraphs.summary: Article 12(2)(a) of the EU AI Act — logging for risk and substantial modification detection. First enumerated logging purpose: the system's log stream must be capable of capturing events that point to either an Article 79(1) risk situation or a substantial modification of the high-risk AI system. Anchors enforcement and corrective-action triggers under Articles 79 (risk handling) and 20 (corrective action).

paragraphs.label: 2(b)
paragraphs.summary: Article 12(2)(b) of the EU AI Act — logging for post-market monitoring. Logging capabilities must enable recording of events relevant to facilitating the post-market monitoring required under Article 72. Feeds the provider's continuous evidence base on in-field performance.

paragraphs.label: 2(c)
paragraphs.summary: Article 12(2)(c) of the EU AI Act — logging for deployer monitoring of operation. Logging must enable recording of events relevant to monitoring the operation of high-risk AI systems referred to in Article 26(5) (deployer monitoring duty). Aligns the system's instrumented signals with what deployers must observe in operation.

Article 12(3) of the EU AI Act — minimum logging for biometric remote identification (Annex III point 1(a)) (chapeau). For high-risk AI systems referred to in Annex III point 1(a) — remote biometric identification systems — logging must provide at least the elements listed in points (a)–(d): usage period, reference database, matched inputs, and identification of verifying persons. Sets a baseline forensic record for the most sensitive Annex III category.

paragraphs.label: 3(a)
paragraphs.summary: Article 12(3)(a) of the EU AI Act — minimum log: usage period. For remote biometric identification systems, logging must include recording of the period of each use of the system, namely the start date and time and the end date and time of each use. Enables session-level reconstruction of when the system was active.

paragraphs.label: 3(b)
paragraphs.summary: Article 12(3)(b) of the EU AI Act — minimum log: reference database. For remote biometric identification systems, logging must capture the reference database against which input data has been checked by the system. Lets supervisors trace which watchlist or gallery a match was drawn against.

paragraphs.label: 3(c)
paragraphs.summary: Article 12(3)(c) of the EU AI Act — minimum log: matched inputs. For remote biometric identification systems, logging must record the input data for which the search has led to a match. Preserves the operative evidence used to drive any downstream identification decision.

paragraphs.label: 3(d)
paragraphs.summary: Article 12(3)(d) of the EU AI Act — minimum log: human verifiers. For remote biometric identification systems, logging must record the identification of the natural persons involved in verifying the results, as referred to in Article 14(5). Anchors accountability of the two-person verification rule for biometric identifications.

articles.summary: Article 12 of the EU AI Act — Record-Keeping. High-risk AI systems must technically allow for the automatic recording of events ('logs') over their lifetime to ensure a level of traceability appropriate to the intended purpose. Logging must enable identification of situations leading to systemic risks, post-market monitoring and the recording of relevant operating data. For Annex III(1)(a) remote biometric identification systems, mandatory log content is specified (period and database of use, input data, identifying personnel). The technical condition that makes Articles 19, 26(6) and 72 enforceable. Applies from 2 August 2026. MVP-critical.

articles.heading: Transparency and Provision of Information to Deployers

paragraphs.summary: Article 13(1) of the EU AI Act — transparency-by-design for high-risk AI systems. High-risk AI systems must be designed and developed so that their operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret the system's output and use it appropriately. The type and degree of transparency must be set with a view to achieving the relevant provider and deployer obligations under Section 3 (notably Article 26 deployer duties).

Article 13(2) of the EU AI Act — instructions for use (general). High-risk AI systems must be accompanied by instructions for use, in an appropriate digital or other format, that include concise, complete, correct and clear information that is relevant, accessible and comprehensible to deployers. The instructions for use are the principal vehicle the provider uses to transfer transparency-relevant information downstream.

Article 13(3) of the EU AI Act — minimum content of instructions for use (chapeau). The instructions for use must contain at least the information set out in points (a)–(f): provider identity, capabilities/limitations (with sub-elements i–vii), predetermined changes, oversight measures, lifecycle/maintenance, and logging mechanisms. Sets a floor — sectoral or contractual obligations may require more.

paragraphs.label: 3(a)
paragraphs.summary: Article 13(3)(a) of the EU AI Act — provider identity in instructions for use. The instructions for use must state the identity and contact details of the provider and, where applicable, of its authorised representative established in the Union. Anchors downstream contactability for incident reporting, corrective actions, and supervisory engagement.

paragraphs.label: 3(b)
paragraphs.summary: Article 13(3)(b) of the EU AI Act — characteristics, capabilities and limitations (chapeau). The instructions for use must describe the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance of the high-risk AI system. The detailed elements are enumerated in sub-points (i) through (vii) under Article 13(3)(b).

paragraphs.label: 3(i)
paragraphs.summary: Article 13(3)(b)(i) of the EU AI Act — intended purpose. The instructions for use must state the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system. Becomes the reference scope against which Article 9 risk identification, Article 10 data suitability, and deployer-side compliance under Article 26(1) are measured.

paragraphs.label: 3(ii)
paragraphs.summary: Article 13(3)(b)(ii) of the EU AI Act — accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity disclosure. The instructions for use must state the level of accuracy (including metrics), robustness and cybersecurity referred to in Article 15 against which the system has been tested and validated, the level that can be expected, and any known or foreseeable circumstances that may impact that expected level.

paragraphs.label: 3(iii)
paragraphs.summary: Article 13(3)(b)(iii) of the EU AI Act — foreseeable risks to health, safety and rights. The instructions for use must describe any known or foreseeable circumstance, related to use in accordance with intended purpose or under reasonably foreseeable misuse, which may lead to risks to health, safety or fundamental rights referred to in Article 9(2). Mirrors Article 9 in the user-facing documentation.

paragraphs.label: 3(iv)
paragraphs.summary: Article 13(3)(b)(iv) of the EU AI Act — output explanation capabilities. Where applicable, the instructions for use must describe the technical capabilities and characteristics of the high-risk AI system to provide information relevant to explain its output. Operationalises explainability disclosure where the system has such features (e.g. attribution scores, rationales).

paragraphs.label: 3(v)
paragraphs.summary: Article 13(3)(b)(v) of the EU AI Act — performance across persons or groups. When appropriate, the instructions for use must describe the system's performance regarding specific persons or groups of persons on whom it is intended to be used. Pushes subgroup performance disclosure into the user documentation, e.g. for demographic slices.

paragraphs.label: 3(vi)
paragraphs.summary: Article 13(3)(b)(vi) of the EU AI Act — input data specifications. When appropriate, the instructions for use must include specifications for input data, or any other relevant information about the training, validation and testing data sets used, having regard to the intended purpose. Lets deployers calibrate operational inputs against the data the system was built on.

paragraphs.label: 3(vii)
paragraphs.summary: Article 13(3)(b)(vii) of the EU AI Act — output interpretation guidance. Where applicable, the instructions for use must include information enabling deployers to interpret the output of the high-risk AI system and use it appropriately. Bridges the technical output back to the deployer's decision-making workflow.

paragraphs.label: 3(c)
paragraphs.summary: Article 13(3)(c) of the EU AI Act — predetermined changes. The instructions for use must describe the changes to the high-risk AI system and its performance that have been predetermined by the provider at the moment of the initial conformity assessment, if any. Anchors the distinction between in-scope updates and a 'substantial modification' that retriggers conformity assessment.

paragraphs.label: 3(d)
paragraphs.summary: Article 13(3)(d) of the EU AI Act — instructions for use: human oversight measures. The instructions for use must describe the Article 14 human-oversight measures, including any technical features the provider has built in to help deployers interpret system outputs. Lets the deployer understand and operationalise the oversight design baked into the system.

paragraphs.label: 3(e)
paragraphs.summary: Article 13(3)(e) of the EU AI Act — instructions for use: resources, lifetime and maintenance. The instructions for use must specify the compute and hardware resources the system needs, its expected lifetime, and the maintenance and care activities (and their frequency) required to keep it functioning correctly — including any necessary software updates. Sets the operational sustainment baseline deployers have to plan around.

paragraphs.label: 3(f)
paragraphs.summary: Article 13(3)(f) of the EU AI Act — log-handling mechanisms. Where relevant, the instructions for use must describe the mechanisms within the high-risk AI system that allow deployers to properly collect, store and interpret the logs in accordance with Article 12. Lets deployers exercise their Article 26(6) retention duty meaningfully.

articles.summary: Article 13 of the EU AI Act — Transparency and Provision of Information to Deployers. High-risk AI systems must be designed and developed so that their operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret outputs and use them appropriately. Providers must supply concise, complete, correct and clear instructions for use covering provider identity, intended purpose, performance characteristics (accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity), known limitations, foreseeable misuse, human oversight measures, computational and hardware resources, expected lifetime and maintenance. Underpins the deployer's ability to discharge Art 26 duties. Applies from 2 August 2026. MVP-critical.

articles.heading: Human Oversight

paragraphs.summary: Article 14(1) of the EU AI Act — human oversight by design. High-risk AI systems must be designed and developed in such a way — including with appropriate human-machine interface tools — that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use. Frames oversight as a built-in design property of the system, not solely an organisational measure at the deployer.

Article 14(2) of the EU AI Act — purpose of human oversight. Human oversight must aim to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety or fundamental rights that may emerge when a high-risk AI system is used as intended or under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse, in particular where such risks persist despite applying the other Section 2 requirements. Positions oversight as the last line of defence after design-time controls.

Article 14(3) of the EU AI Act — proportionate oversight measures (chapeau). The oversight measures must be commensurate with the risks, level of autonomy and context of use of the high-risk AI system. They must be ensured through one or both of the two measure types in (a) and (b): provider-built measures and provider-identified measures to be implemented by the deployer.

paragraphs.label: 3(a)
paragraphs.summary: Article 14(3)(a) of the EU AI Act — provider-built oversight measures. First of the two oversight delivery channels under Article 14(3): oversight measures the provider identifies and, where technically feasible, engineers into the high-risk AI system itself prior to placing on the market or putting into service. Captures design-time controls such as interface elements, stop functions and monitoring hooks built into the product.

paragraphs.label: 3(b)
paragraphs.summary: Article 14(3)(b) of the EU AI Act — provider-identified, deployer-implemented oversight. Oversight may also be ensured through measures identified by the provider before placing the system on the market or putting it into service that are appropriate to be implemented by the deployer. Splits oversight responsibility between provider design and deployer organisational practice.

Article 14(4) of the EU AI Act — capacities the human overseer must have (chapeau). For paragraphs 1–3 to be implemented, the high-risk AI system must be provided to the deployer in such a way that natural persons assigned human oversight can, as appropriate and proportionate, do the things enumerated in points (a)–(e): understand limitations, resist automation bias, interpret outputs, decide not to use the output, and intervene/stop the system.

paragraphs.label: 4(a)
paragraphs.summary: Article 14(4)(a) of the EU AI Act — understanding capacities and limitations. The human overseer must be enabled to properly understand the relevant capacities and limitations of the high-risk AI system and to monitor its operation, including detecting and addressing anomalies, dysfunctions and unexpected performance. Demands more than awareness — meaningful comprehension and observability.

paragraphs.label: 4(b)
paragraphs.summary: Article 14(4)(b) of the EU AI Act — guarding against automation bias. The human overseer must remain aware of the possible tendency of automatically relying or over-relying on the output of a high-risk AI system (automation bias), in particular for systems used to provide information or recommendations for decisions taken by natural persons. Explicit recognition of this oversight failure mode.

paragraphs.label: 4(c)
paragraphs.summary: Article 14(4)(c) of the EU AI Act — correctly interpreting outputs. The human overseer must be able to correctly interpret the high-risk AI system's output, taking into account the interpretation tools and methods available. Demands actual interpretive competence, not just nominal supervision.

paragraphs.label: 4(d)
paragraphs.summary: Article 14(4)(d) of the EU AI Act — power to disregard the output. The natural person assigned oversight must be empowered to choose not to rely on the high-risk AI system in a given case, and to disregard, override or reverse its output. Establishes substantive override authority for the human, not merely a procedural sign-off.

paragraphs.label: 4(e)
paragraphs.summary: Article 14(4)(e) of the EU AI Act — intervention and stop function. The human overseer must be able to intervene in the operation of the high-risk AI system or interrupt the system through a 'stop' button or a similar procedure that brings the system to a halt in a safe state. Concrete kill-switch capability for the last-line oversight role.

Article 14(5) of the EU AI Act — two-person verification for biometric identification. For high-risk AI systems referred to in Annex III point 1(a) (remote biometric identification), oversight measures must additionally ensure that no action or decision is taken by the deployer on the basis of the identification unless that identification has been separately verified and confirmed by at least two natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority. Carve-outs apply for law enforcement, migration, border control and asylum where Union or national law deems this requirement disproportionate.

articles.summary: Article 14 of the EU AI Act — Human Oversight. High-risk AI systems must be designed and developed so they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period they are in use. Oversight measures must aim at preventing or minimising risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, must be commensurate to the risks, and must enable assigned persons to understand capacities and limitations, remain aware of automation bias, correctly interpret outputs, decide not to use the system or override its output, and intervene or stop it. For Annex III(1)(a) remote biometric identification a 'two-person' verification rule applies. Applies from 2 August 2026. MVP-critical.

articles.heading: Accuracy, Robustness and Cybersecurity

paragraphs.summary: Article 15(1) of the EU AI Act — accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity by design. High-risk AI systems must be designed and developed to achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, and to perform consistently on those properties throughout their lifecycle. Sets the three foundational performance pillars whose measurement, declaration and resilience are elaborated in paragraphs 2–5.

Article 15(2) of the EU AI Act — benchmarks and measurement methodologies. The Commission, in cooperation with relevant stakeholders and organisations such as metrology and benchmarking authorities, must as appropriate encourage the development of benchmarks and measurement methodologies for accuracy, robustness and other relevant performance metrics. Builds the standardisation backbone for Article 15(1).

Article 15(3) of the EU AI Act — accuracy declaration in instructions for use. The levels of accuracy and the relevant accuracy metrics of high-risk AI systems must be declared in the accompanying instructions for use. Forces explicit, comparable performance disclosure to deployers; ties back to Article 13(3)(b)(ii).

Article 15(4) of the EU AI Act — robustness against errors and interactions. High-risk AI systems must be as resilient as possible regarding errors, faults or inconsistencies that may occur within the system or the environment, in particular due to interaction with natural persons or other systems. Technical and organisational measures must address robustness, including backup or fail-safe plans. Special attention to feedback loops where outputs of self-learning systems become inputs to future operations, with measures to mitigate biased outputs.

Article 15(5) of the EU AI Act — cybersecurity resilience. High-risk AI systems must be resilient against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter their use, outputs or performance by exploiting system vulnerabilities. Technical solutions must be appropriate to the circumstances and risks. They must include, as appropriate, measures to prevent, detect, respond to, resolve and control AI-specific attacks such as data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples (model evasion), confidentiality attacks and model flaws.

articles.summary: Article 15 of the EU AI Act — Accuracy, Robustness and Cybersecurity. High-risk AI systems must be designed and developed to achieve, in light of their intended purpose, appropriate levels of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, and to perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle. Accuracy metrics and resilience to errors, faults and inconsistencies must be declared. Systems that continue to learn after placing on the market must mitigate feedback-loop bias. Cybersecurity measures must address AI-specific attack vectors: data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples, model evasion and confidentiality attacks. Applies from 2 August 2026. MVP-critical.

articles.heading: Obligations of Providers of High-Risk AI Systems

paragraphs.label: (a)
paragraphs.summary: Article 16(a) of the EU AI Act — provider obligation: compliance with Section 2 requirements. Providers of high-risk AI systems must ensure that their high-risk AI systems are compliant with the requirements set out in Section 2 of Chapter III (Articles 8–15: risk management, data, documentation, logging, transparency, oversight, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity). The cornerstone substantive duty around which Articles 17–21 build the procedural envelope.

paragraphs.label: (b)
paragraphs.summary: Article 16(b) of the EU AI Act — provider obligation: identification on system. Providers must indicate on the high-risk AI system or, where that is not possible, on its packaging or accompanying documentation, their name, registered trade name or registered trade mark, and the address at which they can be contacted. Anchors traceability of the responsible provider.

paragraphs.label: (c)
paragraphs.summary: Article 16(c) of the EU AI Act — provider obligation: quality management system. Providers must have a quality management system in place that complies with Article 17. Operationalises the systemic governance scaffolding under which Article 16's other duties are executed.

paragraphs.label: (d)
paragraphs.summary: Article 16(d) of the EU AI Act — provider obligation: documentation retention. Providers must keep the documentation referred to in Article 18, namely the technical documentation under Article 11, QMS documentation under Article 17, documentation on changes approved by notified bodies, decisions of notified bodies, the EU declaration of conformity, for ten years after placement on the market or putting into service.

paragraphs.label: (e)
paragraphs.summary: Article 16(e) of the EU AI Act — provider obligation: retain logs in provider custody. Providers must retain the logs automatically generated by their high-risk AI systems referred to in Article 19, to the extent those logs are under the provider's control. Captures the share of the Article 12 log stream the provider physically holds, distinct from deployer-side retention under Article 26(6).

paragraphs.label: (f)
paragraphs.summary: Article 16(f) of the EU AI Act — provider obligation: pre-market conformity assessment. Before a high-risk AI system is placed on the market or put into service, its provider must put it through the applicable Article 43 conformity-assessment procedure. The procedural gate connecting Article 16(a)'s substantive compliance duty to market access, and the trigger for notified-body involvement where Article 43 requires it.

paragraphs.label: (g)
paragraphs.summary: Article 16(g) of the EU AI Act — provider obligation: EU declaration of conformity. Providers must draw up an EU declaration of conformity in accordance with Article 47. The formal statement under which the provider takes responsibility for the high-risk AI system's compliance with the Regulation.

paragraphs.label: (h)
paragraphs.summary: Article 16(h) of the EU AI Act — provider obligation: CE marking. Providers must affix the CE marking to the high-risk AI system or, where that is not possible, to its packaging or accompanying documentation, in accordance with Article 48, to indicate conformity with the Regulation. Slots the AI Act into the established EU product-marking regime.

paragraphs.label: (i)
paragraphs.summary: Article 16(i) of the EU AI Act — provider obligation: EU database registration. Providers must comply with the registration obligations referred to in Article 49(1), namely registration of the high-risk AI system in the EU database before placement on the market or putting into service. Drives the public-facing transparency layer of the regime.

paragraphs.label: (j)
paragraphs.summary: Article 16(j) of the EU AI Act — provider obligation: corrective actions and information. Providers must take the necessary corrective actions and provide information as required in Article 20 (e.g. bringing the system into conformity, withdrawing, recalling, disabling, informing distributors, deployers, authorised representatives and importers, and competent authorities). The post-market response duty.

paragraphs.label: (k)
paragraphs.summary: Article 16(k) of the EU AI Act — provider obligation: demonstrate conformity on request. Upon a reasoned request of a national competent authority, providers must demonstrate the conformity of the high-risk AI system with the requirements set out in Section 2. The supervisory cooperation hook into the documentation kept under Article 16(d) and Article 18.

paragraphs.label: (l)
paragraphs.summary: Article 16(l) of the EU AI Act — provider obligation: accessibility conformity. The provider must ensure the high-risk AI system meets the accessibility standards mandated by Directive (EU) 2016/2102 (public-sector web and mobile accessibility) and Directive (EU) 2019/882 (European Accessibility Act). Pulls accessibility compliance inside the AI Act's conformity perimeter rather than leaving it as a sector-only concern.

articles.summary: Article 16 of the EU AI Act — Obligations of Providers of High-Risk AI Systems. The provider's master checklist: ensure compliance with Arts 9–15, indicate provider name and contact on the system or its packaging, operate a quality management system (Art 17), keep documentation (Art 18) and logs (Art 19), undergo conformity assessment (Art 43), draw up the EU declaration of conformity (Art 47) and affix CE marking (Art 48), register in the EU database (Art 49), take corrective action (Art 20), demonstrate compliance on request (Art 21), and meet accessibility requirements. The single anchor for provider duties — Articles 17–21 elaborate each item. MVP-critical.

articles.heading: Quality Management System

paragraphs.summary: Article 17(1) of the EU AI Act — quality management system (chapeau). Providers of high-risk AI systems must put a quality management system (QMS) in place that ensures compliance with the Regulation. It must be documented in a systematic and orderly manner as written policies, procedures and instructions, and must include at least the aspects enumerated in points (a)–(m), spanning regulatory strategy, design, development, testing, standards, data, risk, post-market, incident reporting, communications, record-keeping, resources and accountability.

paragraphs.label: 1(a)
paragraphs.summary: Article 17(1)(a) of the EU AI Act — QMS element: regulatory compliance strategy. The quality management system must cover an internal strategy for achieving regulatory compliance, including how the provider will satisfy applicable conformity-assessment procedures and how modifications to the high-risk AI system will be managed across its lifecycle. Sets the governance plane over Article 43 conformity assessment and substantial-modification handling.

paragraphs.label: 1(b)
paragraphs.summary: Article 17(1)(b) of the EU AI Act — QMS element: design and design verification. The QMS must include techniques, procedures and systematic actions for the design, design control and design verification of the high-risk AI system. Locks design discipline into the QMS scope.

paragraphs.label: 1(c)
paragraphs.summary: Article 17(1)(c) of the EU AI Act — QMS element: development quality. The QMS must include techniques, procedures and systematic actions for the development, quality control and quality assurance of the high-risk AI system. Operational complement to design verification under point (b).

paragraphs.label: 1(d)
paragraphs.summary: Article 17(1)(d) of the EU AI Act — QMS element: examination, test and validation. The quality management system must define the examination, testing and validation procedures applied to the high-risk AI system across pre-development, in-development and post-development stages, and must specify how frequently each is run. Sets the cadence and scope of testing inside the QMS.

paragraphs.label: 1(e)
paragraphs.summary: Article 17(1)(e) of the EU AI Act — QMS element: technical specifications and standards. The QMS must include the technical specifications, including standards, to be applied and, where harmonised standards are not applied in full or do not cover all relevant requirements, the means used to ensure the high-risk AI system complies with Section 2 requirements. Anchors the standards-based compliance pathway.

paragraphs.label: 1(f)
paragraphs.summary: Article 17(1)(f) of the EU AI Act — QMS element: data management. The QMS must include systems and procedures for data management, including data acquisition, collection, analysis, labelling, storage, filtration, mining, aggregation, retention and any other data operation performed before and for the purpose of placing on the market or putting into service the high-risk AI system. Operationalises Article 10 inside the QMS.

paragraphs.label: 1(g)
paragraphs.summary: Article 17(1)(g) of the EU AI Act — QMS element: risk management system. The QMS must encompass the risk management system referred to in Article 9. Folds the Article 9 lifecycle risk process into the broader QMS.

paragraphs.label: 1(h)
paragraphs.summary: Article 17(1)(h) of the EU AI Act — QMS element: post-market monitoring. The QMS must include the setting-up, implementation and maintenance of a post-market monitoring system in accordance with Article 72. Embeds the field-evidence loop inside QMS governance.

paragraphs.label: 1(i)
paragraphs.summary: Article 17(1)(i) of the EU AI Act — QMS element: serious incident reporting. The QMS must include procedures related to the reporting of serious incidents in accordance with Article 73. Operationalises the incident reporting duty inside the QMS.

paragraphs.label: 1(j)
paragraphs.summary: Article 17(1)(j) of the EU AI Act — QMS element: communications. The QMS must include the handling of communication with national competent authorities, other relevant authorities (including those providing or supporting access to data), notified bodies, other operators, customers and other interested parties. Codifies stakeholder communication discipline.

paragraphs.label: 1(k)
paragraphs.summary: Article 17(1)(k) of the EU AI Act — QMS element: record-keeping. The QMS must include systems and procedures for record-keeping of all relevant documentation and information. Pairs with Article 18's retention duty by ensuring the record exists in the first place.

paragraphs.label: 1(l)
paragraphs.summary: Article 17(1)(l) of the EU AI Act — QMS element: resource management. The QMS must include resource management, including security-of-supply related measures. Captures dependencies such as compute, data sources and models that, if disrupted, would compromise compliance.

paragraphs.label: 1(m)
paragraphs.summary: Article 17(1)(m) of the EU AI Act — QMS element: accountability framework. The QMS must articulate an internal accountability framework that allocates, between senior management and other staff, the responsibilities for every aspect listed in Article 17(1)(a)–(l). Forces ownership-mapping so QMS duties are not orphaned across the provider's organisation.

Article 17(2) of the EU AI Act — proportionality to organisation size. Implementation of the aspects in paragraph 1 must be proportionate to the size of the provider's organisation. Providers must in any event respect the degree of rigour and the level of protection required to ensure the compliance of their high-risk AI systems with the Regulation. SMEs get scaling, not a discount on substantive protection.

Article 17(3) of the EU AI Act — integration with sectoral QMS regimes. Providers already operating a quality management system (or an equivalent function) required under sectoral Union law may fold the Article 17(1) aspects into that pre-existing QMS rather than running a parallel AI-specific one. Designed to avoid duplicate QMS regimes for sectors such as medical devices, automotive and aviation.

Article 17(4) of the EU AI Act — financial-institutions carve-out. For providers that are financial institutions subject to internal governance, arrangements or processes requirements under Union financial services law, the obligation to put in place a QMS — with the exception of paragraph 1, points (g), (h) and (i) (risk management, post-market monitoring, serious incident reporting) — is deemed fulfilled by compliance with those financial-services rules. Recognises the equivalence of mature prudential frameworks.

articles.summary: Article 17 of the EU AI Act — Quality Management System. Providers of high-risk AI systems must put in place a documented QMS that ensures compliance with the Regulation, proportionate to the size of the provider. Mandatory elements span: regulatory compliance strategy, design and development control, quality control and assurance, testing and validation procedures, technical specifications, data management, risk management, post-market monitoring, incident reporting (Art 73), communication with authorities, record-keeping, resource and personnel management, and accountability framework. Providers that are financial institutions may integrate the QMS into existing prudential rules. Applies from 2 August 2026. MVP-critical.

articles.heading: Documentation Keeping
articles.summary: Article 18 of the EU AI Act — Documentation Keeping. Providers must keep the technical documentation (Art 11), QMS documentation (Art 17), any documentation on changes approved by notified bodies, the decisions and documents issued by notified bodies, and the EU declaration of conformity at the disposal of national competent authorities for 10 years after the system has been placed on the market or put into service. Special rules where the provider goes bankrupt or ceases activity before that period ends.

articles.heading: Automatically Generated Logs
articles.summary: Article 19 of the EU AI Act — Automatically Generated Logs. Providers of high-risk AI systems must keep the logs referred to in Article 12(1) that are under their control for a period appropriate to the intended purpose — at least six months unless other applicable Union or national law (notably data protection) provides otherwise. Providers that are financial institutions must keep the logs as part of the documentation kept under Union financial-services law.

articles.heading: Corrective Actions and Duty of Information
articles.summary: Article 20 of the EU AI Act — Corrective Actions and Duty of Information. Providers that consider or have reason to consider that a high-risk AI system they have placed on the market or put into service is not in conformity with the Regulation must immediately take the necessary corrective actions (withdraw, disable, recall) and inform distributors, importers, deployers, authorised representatives, and competent authorities. Where the system presents a risk under Art 79(1) the provider must also investigate causes and inform market surveillance and any notified body involved.

articles.heading: Cooperation with Competent Authorities
articles.summary: Article 21 of the EU AI Act — Cooperation with Competent Authorities. On a reasoned request from a competent authority, providers must provide all information and documentation necessary to demonstrate conformity of the high-risk AI system with the requirements in Chapter III Section 2, in an official Union language. Authorities may request access to logs under provider control. Confidentiality of information obtained is protected under Art 78.

articles.heading: Authorised Representatives of Providers of High-Risk AI Systems
articles.summary: Article 22 of the EU AI Act — Authorised Representatives of Providers of High-Risk AI Systems. Providers established outside the Union must, before making their high-risk AI system available on the EU market, appoint by written mandate an authorised representative established in the Union. The representative verifies that the EU declaration of conformity and technical documentation have been drawn up, keeps documentation available for authorities, cooperates with regulators, complies with registration obligations, and may terminate the mandate where the provider acts contrary to the Regulation — in which case it must inform the market surveillance authority and notified body.

articles.heading: Obligations of Importers
articles.summary: Article 23 of the EU AI Act — Obligations of Importers. Before placing a high-risk AI system on the Union market, importers must verify the provider has carried out the relevant conformity assessment, drawn up the technical documentation, affixed CE marking and the EU declaration of conformity, and appointed an authorised representative where required. Importers indicate their name and contact on the system, ensure storage and transport conditions do not jeopardise conformity, keep a copy of the certificate and instructions for 10 years, and cooperate with competent authorities.

articles.heading: Obligations of Distributors
articles.summary: Article 24 of the EU AI Act — Obligations of Distributors. Before making a high-risk AI system available, distributors must verify it bears the required CE marking, is accompanied by the EU declaration of conformity and instructions for use, and that the provider and importer have complied with their respective obligations under Arts 16 and 23. Distributors must ensure storage and transport conditions preserve compliance, take corrective action where they consider the system non-conforming, and inform providers, importers and authorities. Cooperation duties mirror those of importers.

articles.heading: Responsibilities Along the AI Value Chain
articles.summary: Article 25 of the EU AI Act — Responsibilities Along the AI Value Chain. The 'provider flip': any distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is treated as the provider of a high-risk AI system (with all Art 16 obligations) if it (a) puts its name or trademark on it, (b) makes a substantial modification while keeping it high-risk, or (c) modifies the intended purpose of an AI system not previously classified as high-risk so that it becomes high-risk. The original provider's duties shift accordingly. Art 25(4) also requires upstream third-party suppliers of tools, services, components or processes to support downstream compliance by written agreement (the 'API/model-supplier' clause).

articles.heading: Obligations of Deployers of High-Risk AI Systems

paragraphs.summary: Article 26(1) of the EU AI Act — deployer duty to use within the instructions for use. Deployers of high-risk AI systems are required to put in place appropriate technical and organisational controls so the system is operated in line with the accompanying instructions for use, subject to the qualifications in Article 26(3) and (6). First and load-bearing duty on the deployer side; ties deployer conduct directly to the Article 13 documentation the provider must supply.

Article 26(2) of the EU AI Act — assigning human oversight. Deployers must assign human oversight of the high-risk AI system to natural persons who have the necessary competence, training and authority, as well as the necessary support. Operationalises Article 14 on the deployer side: the overseer must be empowered, not just designated.

Article 26(3) of the EU AI Act — interaction with other deployer duties. The obligations in paragraphs 1 and 2 are without prejudice to other deployer obligations under Union or national law, and to the deployer's freedom to organise its own resources and activities for the purpose of implementing the human oversight measures indicated by the provider. Preserves overlapping legal regimes (e.g. GDPR, employment law).

Article 26(4) of the EU AI Act — input data quality where deployer controls inputs. Where the deployer exercises control over input data to a high-risk AI system, the deployer must ensure that data is relevant and sufficiently representative for the system's intended purpose. Operates without prejudice to Article 26(1)–(2). Pushes a subset of the provider-side Article 10 data-quality discipline downstream to the deployment context.

Article 26(5) of the EU AI Act — operational monitoring and incident escalation by deployers. Deployers must actively monitor the system in operation against the instructions for use and feed information back to providers under Article 72. If they identify an Article 79(1)-level risk, they must promptly notify the provider or distributor and the competent market surveillance authority, and suspend use. Serious incidents trigger immediate notification — first to the provider, then to the importer/distributor and the market surveillance authority. Carve-outs: Article 73 applies where the provider is unreachable; the duty does not extend to sensitive operational data of law-enforcement deployers; and financial-institution deployers can rely on their financial-services internal-governance regime to discharge the monitoring duty.

Article 26(6) of the EU AI Act — minimum log retention period for deployers. Deployers must retain the automatic logs produced by a high-risk AI system that fall within their control, for a duration appropriate to the system's intended purpose, with a six-month floor unless EU or national law (notably data protection law) sets a different period. Financial-institution deployers integrate the logs into the records they already keep under financial-services law.

Article 26(7) of the EU AI Act — workplace deployment notification duty. Employer-deployers must notify workers' representatives and the workers themselves that they will be subject to a high-risk AI system before it is put into service or used at the workplace. The notification has to follow the procedures established by applicable Union or national law and practice on worker information and consultation. Stacks on top of, and does not displace, sectoral information and consultation regimes.

Article 26(8) of the EU AI Act — public-sector deployer registration and non-use rule. Public-authority deployers — including EU institutions, bodies, offices and agencies — of high-risk AI systems must comply with the registration duties in Article 49. If such a deployer discovers that the high-risk AI system it plans to use is not registered in the EU database, it must refrain from using the system and notify the provider or distributor.

Article 26(9) of the EU AI Act — DPIA reuse. Where applicable, deployers of high-risk AI systems must use the information provided under Article 13 of the AI Act to comply with their obligation to carry out a data protection impact assessment under GDPR Article 35 or Article 27 of Directive (EU) 2016/680. Hardcodes the bridge between the provider's instructions for use and the deployer's DPIA.

Article 26(10) of the EU AI Act — judicial authorisation regime for post-remote biometric identification. Where a deployer uses a high-risk AI system for post-remote biometric identification in the context of an investigation targeting a specific person suspected or convicted of a criminal offence, the deployer must seek authorisation from a judicial — or binding, judicially-reviewable administrative — authority, either ex ante or, exceptionally, within 48 hours. If authorisation is refused, the deployer must immediately cease use and delete the personal data, outputs and results. Applies without prejudice to Directive (EU) 2016/680 on law-enforcement data protection.

Article 26(11) of the EU AI Act — affected-person notification by Annex III deployers. Where an Annex III high-risk AI system is used by a deployer to make or support decisions about natural persons, those natural persons must be told that a high-risk AI system is being used on them. Applies without prejudice to the broader Article 50 transparency regime. For law-enforcement deployments the notification regime is the one in Article 13 of Directive (EU) 2016/680, not this paragraph.

Article 26(12) of the EU AI Act — deployer duty to cooperate with competent authorities. A catch-all duty obliging deployers to cooperate with any action competent authorities take in relation to the high-risk AI system for the purpose of implementing the Regulation. Supports market surveillance, investigation, corrective-action and enforcement activity downstream of placement on the market.

articles.summary: Article 26 of the EU AI Act — Obligations of Deployers of High-Risk AI Systems. Deployers must take appropriate technical and organisational measures to use systems in accordance with instructions, assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence and authority, ensure input data is relevant and sufficiently representative for the intended purpose, monitor operation and inform providers of risks or serious incidents, keep logs under their control for at least six months, inform workers and their representatives before deployment in the workplace, register in the EU database where applicable, conduct a DPIA where Art 35 GDPR applies, and inform natural persons subject to decisions assisted by the system. Specific transparency duties apply for post-remote-biometric-identification by law enforcement. Applies from 2 August 2026. MVP-critical.

articles.heading: Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment for High-Risk AI Systems
articles.summary: Article 27 of the EU AI Act — Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment for High-Risk AI Systems. Before deploying certain high-risk AI systems (in particular Annex III systems used by bodies governed by public law, private operators providing public services, and Annex III(5)(b)–(c) credit scoring and life/health insurance) deployers must perform an FRIA covering: the deployment processes the system will be used in, the period and frequency of use, the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected, the specific harms likely to affect them, the human oversight measures, and the measures to take when those risks materialise. Results notified to the market surveillance authority via a template.

articles.heading: Notifying Authorities
articles.summary: Article 28 of the EU AI Act — Notifying Authorities. Each Member State must designate or establish at least one notifying authority responsible for setting up and carrying out the procedures necessary to assess, designate, notify and monitor conformity assessment bodies. The authority must be objective, impartial, independent of conformity assessment bodies, organisationally separated, staffed with competent personnel, and not offer or perform conformity assessment activities itself.

articles.heading: Application of a Conformity Assessment Body for Notification
articles.summary: Article 29 of the EU AI Act — Application of a Conformity Assessment Body for Notification. Sets the application package a conformity assessment body must submit to the notifying authority of the Member State where it is established to be designated as a notified body under the AI Act: description of activities, AI systems covered, attestation of competence, and accreditation certificate where available (or equivalent documentary evidence).
