Includes the duty to keep the application up to date.

articles.heading: Notification Procedure
articles.summary: Article 30 of the EU AI Act — Notification Procedure. Notifying authorities may only notify conformity assessment bodies that satisfy the requirements of Article 31. Notification is submitted to the Commission and other Member States via NANDO (the Commission's electronic notification tool), accompanied by full details of the conformity assessment activities, modules and AI systems concerned, and the relevant attestation of competence. Objections may be raised within set periods; notification takes effect after publication when no objections are pending.

articles.heading: Requirements Relating to Notified Bodies
articles.summary: Article 31 of the EU AI Act — Requirements Relating to Notified Bodies. Notified bodies must be established under national law with legal personality, organisationally and financially independent of the providers they assess and of competitors, free from conflicts of interest (with detailed personnel restrictions), able to perform tasks impartially and confidentially, technically and methodologically competent in AI, equipped with adequate staff and infrastructure, and covered by liability insurance unless the State assumes liability. They must participate in or be informed by relevant standardisation.

articles.heading: Presumption of Conformity with Requirements Relating to Notified Bodies
articles.summary: Article 32 of the EU AI Act — Presumption of Conformity with Requirements Relating to Notified Bodies. Where a conformity assessment body demonstrates conformity with the criteria laid down in the relevant harmonised standards (or parts thereof) whose references have been published in the Official Journal, it is presumed to comply with the requirements set out in Article 31 to the extent the standards cover those requirements. A standards-based shortcut for showing CAB qualification.

articles.heading: Subsidiaries of Notified Bodies and Subcontracting
articles.summary: Article 33 of the EU AI Act — Subsidiaries of Notified Bodies and Subcontracting. Where a notified body subcontracts specific tasks or uses a subsidiary, it must ensure the subcontractor or subsidiary meets the Art 31 requirements and inform the notifying authority. Activities may only be subcontracted with the client's agreement. Full responsibility remains with the notified body, which must keep at the disposal of the notifying authority documents concerning the qualifications and work carried out under the subcontract.

articles.heading: Operational Obligations of Notified Bodies
articles.summary: Article 34 of the EU AI Act — Operational Obligations of Notified Bodies. Notified bodies must verify conformity in accordance with the procedures of Article 43, avoid unnecessary burdens for providers, take due account of size (especially SMEs and start-ups) and sector, follow agreed practices, ensure proportionality, and maintain confidentiality. They must keep the notifying authority informed of any changes to their organisation and conformity assessment activities and refrain from acts that could undermine confidence in independence.

articles.heading: Identification Numbers and Lists of Notified Bodies
articles.summary: Article 35 of the EU AI Act — Identification Numbers and Lists of Notified Bodies. The Commission assigns a single identification number to each notified body — even where a body is notified under several Union acts. The Commission publishes the list of notified bodies under the AI Act, including their identification numbers and the activities for which they have been notified, and keeps it up to date in NANDO.

articles.heading: Changes to Notifications
articles.summary: Article 36 of the EU AI Act — Changes to Notifications. The notifying authority must inform the Commission and other Member States of any relevant changes to a notification. Procedures for restricting, suspending or withdrawing notification — including where a notified body no longer meets requirements or has failed to fulfil obligations — and the consequences for outstanding certificates (transfer, validity, surveillance) are set out, together with appeal rights.

articles.heading: Challenge to the Competence of Notified Bodies
articles.summary: Article 37 of the EU AI Act — Challenge to the Competence of Notified Bodies. The Commission must investigate cases where it has reason to doubt the competence of a notified body or the ongoing fulfilment of requirements, and inform the notifying Member State of the findings. The Member State must take the necessary corrective measures, including withdrawal of the notification if needed. Establishes EU-level supervision over national notification decisions.

articles.heading: Coordination of Notified Bodies
articles.summary: Article 38 of the EU AI Act — Coordination of Notified Bodies. The Commission ensures that appropriate coordination and cooperation among notified bodies active in the conformity assessment of AI systems is put in place and properly operated in the form of a sectoral group. Member States must ensure their notified bodies participate, directly or through designated representatives, in the work of that group.

articles.heading: Conformity Assessment Bodies of Third Countries
articles.summary: Article 39 of the EU AI Act — Conformity Assessment Bodies of Third Countries. Conformity assessment bodies established under the law of a third country with which the Union has concluded an agreement may be authorised to carry out AI Act conformity-assessment activities, provided they meet Article 31 requirements or ensure an equivalent level of compliance.

articles.heading: Harmonised Standards and Standardisation Deliverables
articles.summary: Article 40 of the EU AI Act — Harmonised Standards and Standardisation Deliverables. High-risk AI systems or general-purpose AI models that are in conformity with harmonised standards (or parts thereof) the references of which are published in the Official Journal of the EU are presumed to comply with the relevant requirements of Chapter III Section 2 (or Arts 53 and 55 for GPAI) to the extent the standards cover those requirements. The Commission issues standardisation requests to CEN/CENELEC and may request the European AI Board's input. The primary route to demonstrating conformity for non-Annex-I providers.

articles.heading: Common Specifications
articles.summary: Article 41 of the EU AI Act — Common Specifications. Where harmonised standards do not exist, are insufficient, or fail to address specific safety or fundamental-rights concerns, the Commission may adopt by implementing act common specifications providing technical solutions. Compliance with common specifications gives the same presumption of conformity as harmonised standards. Providers that do not apply common specifications must justify they have adopted technical solutions providing an equivalent level of compliance.

articles.heading: Presumption of Conformity with Certain Requirements
articles.summary: Article 42 of the EU AI Act — Presumption of Conformity with Certain Requirements. High-risk AI systems that have been trained and tested on data reflecting the specific geographical, behavioural, contextual or functional setting in which they are intended to be used are presumed to comply with the Article 10(4) data-governance requirement. High-risk AI systems certified or for which a statement of conformity has been issued under a cybersecurity scheme pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2019/881 (Cybersecurity Act) are presumed to comply with the Article 15 cybersecurity requirement to the extent the certificate covers it.

articles.heading: Conformity Assessment
articles.summary: Article 43 of the EU AI Act — Conformity Assessment. Determines which procedure a provider of a high-risk AI system must follow. For Annex III(1) biometrics where harmonised standards/common specifications have not been applied (or only partially), third-party assessment via Annex VII is required; otherwise internal control via Annex VI is permitted. For all other Annex III use cases, providers follow internal control (Annex VI). For Annex I products, the AI Act assessment is integrated into the relevant sectoral procedure. The provider must repeat the assessment when the system is substantially modified, even if intended for further use.

articles.heading: Certificates
articles.summary: Article 44 of the EU AI Act — Certificates. Certificates issued by notified bodies under Annex VII must be drawn up in a language easily understood by the relevant authorities, be valid for the period indicated (not exceeding five years for Annex III systems, four years for Annex I products), be renewable on application following re-assessment, and may be suspended, withdrawn or restricted where the system no longer meets requirements or the provider fails to comply with conditions attached to the certificate.

articles.heading: Information Obligations of Notified Bodies
articles.summary: Article 45 of the EU AI Act — Information Obligations of Notified Bodies. Notified bodies must inform the notifying authority of EU technical documentation assessment certificates issued or withdrawn, any refusal, restriction, suspension or withdrawal of a certificate, any circumstances affecting the scope or conditions of notification, requests from market surveillance authorities, and on request, the conformity assessment activities carried out, including cross-border activities and subcontracting.

articles.heading: Derogation from Conformity Assessment Procedure
articles.summary: Article 46 of the EU AI Act — Derogation from Conformity Assessment Procedure. By way of derogation from Article 43 and on duly justified grounds of public security, the protection of life and health, environmental protection, or the protection of critical infrastructure, a market surveillance authority may authorise the placing on the market or putting into service of specific high-risk AI systems within the Member State's territory for a limited period while the procedures are being carried out. Emergency authorisation by law enforcement and civil-protection authorities is permitted without prior authorisation in narrow cases.

articles.heading: EU Declaration of Conformity
articles.summary: Article 47 of the EU AI Act — EU Declaration of Conformity. The provider must draw up a written, machine-readable, physical or electronically signed EU declaration of conformity for each high-risk AI system, keep it at the disposal of national competent authorities for 10 years and translate it into the language(s) required by the Member State where the system is placed. Annex V prescribes content. By drawing up the declaration, the provider assumes responsibility for compliance with the AI Act.

articles.heading: CE Marking
articles.summary: Article 48 of the EU AI Act — CE Marking. CE marking must be affixed visibly, legibly and indelibly to high-risk AI systems before they are placed on the market or put into service (or, where impossible, on the packaging and accompanying documentation). For digital-only AI systems, a digital CE marking is used. Where applicable the CE marking is followed by the identification number of the notified body responsible for Annex VII conformity assessment. General principles of Regulation (EC) No 765/2008 apply.

articles.heading: Registration
articles.summary: Article 49 of the EU AI Act — Registration. Before placing on the market or putting into service a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III (excluding Annex III(2) critical-infrastructure systems), the provider — or where applicable the authorised representative — must register itself and the system in the EU database referred to in Article 71. Deployers that are public authorities or Union institutions, agencies or bodies, and certain private deployers acting on their behalf, must also register their use. Annex VIII sets the information fields.

articles.heading: Transparency Obligations for Providers and Deployers of Certain AI Systems

paragraphs.summary: Article 50(1) of the EU AI Act — disclosure that the user is interacting with an AI. Providers must ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed so that the natural persons concerned are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the point of view of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect, taking into account context and use. Does not apply to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences subject to safeguards for the rights of third parties, unless those systems are available to the public to report a criminal offence.

Article 50(2) of the EU AI Act — machine-readable marking of synthetic content. Provider-side obligation for any AI system (including general-purpose AI) that generates synthetic audio, image, video or text: outputs must be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. Technical solutions must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable to the extent technically feasible, calibrated against the state of the art and cost. Carve-outs: assistive functions for standard editing, systems that do not substantially alter the deployer's input data or semantics, and uses authorised by law for the detection, prevention, investigation or prosecution of criminal offences.

Article 50(3) of the EU AI Act — emotion-recognition and biometric-categorisation disclosure. Deployers of an emotion recognition system or a biometric categorisation system must inform the natural persons exposed thereto of the operation of the system, and must process personal data in accordance with GDPR (Regulation 2016/679), Regulation 2018/1725 and Directive 2016/680 as applicable. The obligation does not apply to AI systems used for biometric categorisation and emotion recognition that are permitted by law to detect, prevent or investigate criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights of third parties and in accordance with Union law.

Article 50(4) of the EU AI Act — deep-fake and AI-generated public-interest text disclosure by deployers. Two deployer-side disclosure duties bundled into one paragraph. First: deployers of an AI system producing or manipulating image, audio or video deep fakes must disclose the artificial origin of that content; for evidently artistic, creative, satirical or fictional works the disclosure is scaled back to an appropriate notice that does not impair the work's enjoyment. Second: deployers of AI systems producing or manipulating text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must disclose the artificial origin, unless the output has been through human review or editorial control with a natural or legal person bearing editorial responsibility. Both duties carve out uses authorised by law for detecting, preventing, investigating or prosecuting criminal offences.

Article 50(5) of the EU AI Act — timing and accessibility of disclosures. The information referred to in paragraphs 1 to 4 must be provided to the natural persons concerned in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure. The information must conform to the applicable accessibility requirements. Anchors usability and timing baselines for all Article 50 transparency duties.

Article 50(6) of the EU AI Act — relationship with Chapter III and other transparency law. Paragraphs 1 to 4 do not affect the requirements and obligations set out in Chapter III (high-risk AI systems) and are without prejudice to other transparency obligations laid down in Union or national law for deployers of AI systems. Confirms Article 50 is a floor, not a ceiling.

Article 50(7) of the EU AI Act — codes of practice on AI-generated content detection. The AI Office must encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of practice at Union level to facilitate the effective implementation of the obligations regarding detection and labelling of artificially generated or manipulated content. The Commission may adopt implementing acts to approve those codes of practice in accordance with the procedure laid down in Article 56(6); if it deems the codes inadequate, the Commission may adopt an implementing act specifying common rules for the implementation of those obligations.

articles.summary: Article 50 of the EU AI Act — Transparency Obligations for Providers and Deployers of Certain AI Systems. The 'limited-risk' transparency layer applied regardless of high-risk classification: providers must design AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons so persons are informed they are interacting with an AI (50(1)); providers of generative AI must mark synthetic audio, image, video or text output as artificially generated or manipulated in a machine-readable format (50(2)); deployers of emotion-recognition or biometric-categorisation systems must inform exposed natural persons (50(3)); deployers of deepfakes must disclose that content has been artificially generated or manipulated (50(4)), with carve-outs for art, satire and law enforcement. Applies from 2 August 2026. MVP-critical.

articles.heading: Classification of General-Purpose AI Models as General-Purpose AI Models with Systemic Risk
articles.summary: Article 51 of the EU AI Act — Classification of General-Purpose AI Models as General-Purpose AI Models with Systemic Risk. A GPAI model is classified as having systemic risk where it has high-impact capabilities evaluated based on appropriate technical tools and methodologies (Art 51(1)(a)) or where, on a Commission decision ex officio or following a scientific-panel alert, it is determined to have capabilities or impact equivalent to (a). The presumption threshold: training compute greater than 10^25 FLOPs (Art 51(2)). The classification gateway to Article 55.

articles.heading: Procedure
articles.summary: Article 52 of the EU AI Act — Procedure. The notification mechanism for GPAI models with systemic risk: providers must notify the Commission without delay (and in any event within two weeks) where their model meets or will meet the Article 51(1)(a) condition. The notification can be accompanied by sufficiently substantiated arguments demonstrating that exceptionally the model does not present systemic risks. The Commission decides; classified models are added to a published list.

articles.heading: Obligations for Providers of General-Purpose AI Models
articles.summary: Article 53 of the EU AI Act — Obligations for Providers of General-Purpose AI Models. Baseline duties for every GPAI model placed on the EU market: draw up and keep up to date technical documentation (Annex XI) for the AI Office and national authorities, draw up and make available information and documentation to downstream providers integrating the model into their AI systems (Annex XII), put in place a policy to comply with Union copyright law including identification and respect of opt-outs under Art 4(3) CDSM Directive, and publish a sufficiently detailed public summary of training content using a Commission-template. Free and open-source models with publicly available weights and architecture are partially exempt, except for systemic-risk models. Applies from 2 August 2025.

articles.heading: Authorised Representatives of Providers of General-Purpose AI Models
articles.summary: Article 54 of the EU AI Act — Authorised Representatives of Providers of General-Purpose AI Models. GPAI model providers established in third countries must, before placing a model on the EU market, appoint by written mandate an authorised representative established in the Union. The representative verifies that Annex XI documentation has been drawn up and Article 53 obligations fulfilled, keeps documentation available, cooperates with the AI Office, and may terminate the mandate where the provider acts contrary to the Regulation. Applies from 2 August 2025.

articles.heading: Obligations for Providers of General-Purpose AI Models with Systemic Risk
articles.summary: Article 55 of the EU AI Act — Obligations for Providers of General-Purpose AI Models with Systemic Risk. In addition to Article 53 duties, providers of GPAI models with systemic risk must perform model evaluation in accordance with state-of-the-art protocols including adversarial testing, assess and mitigate possible systemic risks at Union level, keep track of and report serious incidents and corrective measures to the AI Office and national competent authorities, and ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure. May rely on codes of practice (Art 56) or harmonised standards (Art 40) for presumption of compliance. Applies from 2 August 2025.

articles.heading: Codes of Practice
articles.summary: Article 56 of the EU AI Act — Codes of Practice. The AI Office encourages and facilitates the drawing up of codes of practice at Union level to contribute to the proper application of the Regulation for GPAI models, taking into account international approaches. Codes should cover the means to ensure the Art 53 and Art 55 obligations are met, including model evaluation methods, risk assessment and mitigation, taxonomy of systemic risks, and transparency. The AI Office and the Board may invite GPAI providers, downstream providers, civil society, academia and other experts. Adequacy may be approved by the Commission via implementing act.

articles.heading: AI Regulatory Sandboxes
articles.summary: Article 57 of the EU AI Act — AI Regulatory Sandboxes. Member States must establish at least one AI regulatory sandbox at national level, operational by 2 August 2026, which can also be jointly established with other Member States or as a regional sandbox. Sandboxes provide a controlled environment that fosters innovation and facilitates the development, training, testing and validation of innovative AI systems before they are placed on the market or put into service. Aims include legal certainty, sharing best practices, fostering innovation and competitiveness, contributing to evidence-based regulatory learning, and facilitating SME/start-up access. Free of charge for SMEs except recoverable exceptional costs.

articles.heading: Detailed Arrangements for, and Functioning of, AI Regulatory Sandboxes
articles.summary: Article 58 of the EU AI Act — Detailed Arrangements for, and Functioning of, AI Regulatory Sandboxes. The Commission adopts implementing acts specifying the detailed arrangements for the establishment, development, implementation, operation and supervision of sandboxes. Common principles include eligibility, application, selection, participation, exit, sandbox plans, rights and obligations of participants, monitoring, reporting and termination. Providers in the sandbox remain liable under Union and national liability law for harm inflicted on third parties; substantial cooperation with national authorities and the requirement that any natural-person test data is justified are central.

articles.heading: Further Processing of Personal Data for Developing Certain AI Systems in the Public Interest in the AI Regulatory Sandbox
articles.summary: Article 59 of the EU AI Act — Further Processing of Personal Data for Developing Certain AI Systems in the Public Interest in the AI Regulatory Sandbox. Creates a narrow legal basis under Articles 6(4) and 9(2)(g) GDPR for processing personal data lawfully collected for other purposes when used in the sandbox to develop, train and test AI systems for substantial public interest (public safety, public health, environmental protection, energy, transport, mobility, critical infrastructure, efficiency of public administration). Strict safeguards apply: effective monitoring, isolation, no transmission outside the sandbox, deletion after participation, logs, and a publicly accessible summary of the project.

articles.heading: Testing of High-Risk AI Systems in Real World Conditions Outside AI Regulatory Sandboxes
articles.summary: Article 60 of the EU AI Act — Testing of High-Risk AI Systems in Real World Conditions Outside AI Regulatory Sandboxes. Allows providers (or prospective providers) of Annex III high-risk AI systems to test them in real-world conditions outside sandboxes, subject to a testing plan submitted to the market surveillance authority of the Member State where testing occurs (deemed approved after 30 days unless objected), maximum duration (six months, extendable by six), informed consent of subjects (Art 61), registration in the EU database, oversight by natural persons, and the ability of subjects to withdraw and have data deleted. Serious incidents must be reported.

articles.heading: Informed Consent to Participate in Testing in Real World Conditions Outside AI Regulatory Sandboxes
articles.summary: Article 61 of the EU AI Act — Informed Consent to Participate in Testing in Real World Conditions Outside AI Regulatory Sandboxes. Subjects participating in real-world testing under Art 60 must give freely-given, specific, unambiguous and prior informed consent (or, for vulnerable persons, the consent of their legal representative). The information must include the nature and objectives of testing, conditions, foreseeable inconveniences and risks, expected duration, contact details, the right to withdraw at any time without detriment and to request deletion of personal data, and any compensation. Consent must be documented and given a copy provided to the subject.

articles.heading: Measures for Providers and Deployers, in Particular SMEs, Including Start-Ups
articles.summary: Article 62 of the EU AI Act — Measures for Providers and Deployers, in Particular SMEs, Including Start-Ups. Member States must provide SMEs and start-ups established in the Union with priority access to sandboxes (subject to eligibility), organise awareness and training activities tailored to their needs, use existing dedicated channels for communication, and where appropriate, set fees for conformity assessment under Art 43 proportionate to their size, market stage and economic viability. The Commission supports a single information platform and standardised templates.

articles.heading: Derogations for Specific Operators
articles.summary: Article 63 of the EU AI Act — Derogations for Specific Operators. Microenterprises within the meaning of Recommendation 2003/361/EC may comply with certain elements of the quality management system required by Article 17 in a simplified manner, provided they do not have partner or linked enterprises within the meaning of that Recommendation. The simplification cannot reduce the level of protection or the need to comply with other obligations under the Regulation.

articles.heading: AI Office
articles.summary: Article 64 of the EU AI Act — AI Office. The Commission develops Union expertise and capabilities in the field of AI through the AI Office. Member States must facilitate its tasks. The AI Office is the central EU-level body for monitoring and enforcement of GPAI rules (Arts 88–94), supporting codes of practice (Art 56), contributing to international cooperation and coordination, and assisting the Board, Member States and competent authorities.

articles.heading: Establishment and Structure of the European Artificial Intelligence Board
articles.summary: Article 65 of the EU AI Act — Establishment and Structure of the European Artificial Intelligence Board. Establishes the AI Board composed of one representative per Member State, with the European Data Protection Supervisor as observer. The AI Office attends without voting. The Board adopts rules of procedure by simple majority, including operating rules for sub-groups. Two standing sub-groups address market surveillance and notified bodies. The Board's chair is elected from Member-State representatives.

articles.heading: Tasks of the Board
articles.summary: Article 66 of the EU AI Act — Tasks of the Board. The Board advises and assists the Commission and the Member States to facilitate consistent and effective application of the Regulation. Tasks include contributing to coordination among national authorities, harmonising administrative practices, issuing recommendations and opinions on common specifications, harmonised standards, guidelines, delegated and implementing acts, and the operation of sandboxes, collecting and sharing best practices, and supporting the AI Office on GPAI matters.

articles.heading: Advisory Forum
articles.summary: Article 67 of the EU AI Act — Advisory Forum. Establishes an advisory forum to provide technical expertise and advise the Board and the Commission, with balanced representation from industry, start-ups, SMEs, civil society and academia. The Forum prepares opinions, recommendations and written contributions on request, may establish standing or temporary sub-groups, meets at least twice a year, and its members are appointed for two-year renewable terms.

articles.heading: Scientific Panel of Independent Experts
articles.summary: Article 68 of the EU AI Act — Scientific Panel of Independent Experts. The Commission establishes a Scientific Panel of independent experts selected on the basis of up-to-date scientific or technical expertise in AI, providing support to the AI Office's enforcement of GPAI rules — including by alerting the AI Office to possible systemic risks (Art 90), contributing to model evaluations (Art 92), and developing tools and methodologies for assessing capabilities. Independence, impartiality, transparency and confidentiality obligations apply.

articles.heading: Access to the Pool of Experts by the Member States
articles.summary: Article 69 of the EU AI Act — Access to the Pool of Experts by the Member States. Member States may call upon experts from the Scientific Panel to support their enforcement activities under the Regulation, subject to fees that the Commission sets by implementing act. The fees ensure adequate funding and remuneration of experts and may differ depending on the type of support requested.

articles.heading: Designation of National Competent Authorities and Single Point of Contact
articles.summary: Article 70 of the EU AI Act — Designation of National Competent Authorities and Single Point of Contact. Each Member State must designate at least one notifying authority and at least one market surveillance authority as national competent authorities for the purposes of the Regulation, and identify a single point of contact for communication with the public and counterparts in other Member States and at Union level. Authorities must have adequate technical, financial and human resources, including AI competence, and act independently, objectively and impartially. Member States communicate the designations to the Commission and make them publicly available by 2 August 2025.

articles.heading: EU Database for High-Risk AI Systems Listed in Annex III
articles.summary: Article 71 of the EU AI Act — EU Database for High-Risk AI Systems Listed in Annex III. The Commission, in collaboration with Member States, sets up and maintains an EU database containing the information referred to in Annex VIII on high-risk AI systems registered under Article 49 and on systems not classified as high-risk under Article 6(3). The database is publicly accessible (except for sections concerning law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control) and user-friendly, navigable and machine-readable.

articles.heading: Post-Market Monitoring by Providers and Post-Market Monitoring Plan for High-Risk AI Systems
articles.summary: Article 72 of the EU AI Act — Post-Market Monitoring by Providers and Post-Market Monitoring Plan for High-Risk AI Systems. Providers must establish and document a post-market monitoring system proportionate to the nature of the AI system and the risks, that actively and systematically collects, documents and analyses data on performance throughout the lifetime, and allows evaluation of continuous compliance with Chapter III Section 2 requirements. The Commission adopts an implementing act with a template for the plan. For systems covered by Annex I sectoral law, monitoring may be integrated into existing systems.

articles.heading: Reporting of Serious Incidents
articles.summary: Article 73 of the EU AI Act — Reporting of Serious Incidents. Providers of high-risk AI systems placed on the Union market must report any serious incident to the market surveillance authorities of the Member States where that incident occurred — immediately after the provider has established a causal link or the reasonable likelihood of such a link, and in any event not later than 15 days after becoming aware. Shorter deadlines apply for incidents involving widespread infringement, serious and irreversible disruption to critical infrastructure (2 days), or death of a person (10 days). Providers must investigate, take corrective measures and cooperate with authorities.

articles.heading: Market Surveillance and Control of AI Systems in the Union Market
articles.summary: Article 74 of the EU AI Act — Market Surveillance and Control of AI Systems in the Union Market. Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 applies to AI systems covered by this Regulation. Market surveillance authorities have powers to access documentation, datasets and training, validation and testing datasets, including through APIs or other technical means, source code where strictly necessary, and to carry out unannounced inspections. Specific rules apply to systems used by law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control authorities and to financial-services providers (existing competent authority remains responsible).

articles.heading: Mutual Assistance, Market Surveillance and Control of General-Purpose AI Systems
articles.summary: Article 75 of the EU AI Act — Mutual Assistance, Market Surveillance and Control of General-Purpose AI Systems. Where an AI system is based on a general-purpose AI model and the model and system are developed by the same provider, the AI Office has powers to monitor and supervise the system. National market surveillance authorities may request the AI Office to exercise those powers and to share information; the AI Office may conclude that a system fails to comply due to the underlying model and refer enforcement to national authorities.

articles.heading: Supervision of Testing in Real World Conditions by Market Surveillance Authorities
articles.summary: Article 76 of the EU AI Act — Supervision of Testing in Real World Conditions by Market Surveillance Authorities. Market surveillance authorities have the competence and powers to ensure that testing in real-world conditions complies with the Regulation. They monitor testing, may carry out inspections and require corrective actions, and may suspend or terminate testing where conditions are not met or the risks are unacceptable. Vulnerable subjects receive specific protections.

articles.heading: Powers of Authorities Protecting Fundamental Rights
articles.summary: Article 77 of the EU AI Act — Powers of Authorities Protecting Fundamental Rights. National public authorities or bodies that supervise or enforce respect of obligations under Union law protecting fundamental rights, including the right to non-discrimination, in relation to the use of Annex III high-risk AI systems, have the power to request and access any documentation created or maintained under the Regulation when necessary for effective fulfilment of their mandates. They notify the market surveillance authority of the Member State concerned. The list of designated bodies is published and notified to the Commission.

articles.heading: Confidentiality
articles.summary: Article 78 of the EU AI Act — Confidentiality. The Commission, market surveillance authorities, notified bodies and any other natural or legal person involved in the application of the Regulation must respect the confidentiality of information and data obtained in carrying out their tasks, in particular intellectual property rights, confidential business information and trade secrets, the effective implementation of the Regulation (especially inspections), and the security and integrity of cybersecurity systems and source code. Specific carve-outs allow information sharing across Member States and with the Commission.

articles.heading: Procedure at National Level for Dealing with AI Systems Presenting a Risk
articles.summary: Article 79 of the EU AI Act — Procedure at National Level for Dealing with AI Systems Presenting a Risk. Where a market surveillance authority has sufficient reason to consider that an AI system presents a risk (to health, safety or fundamental rights), it must carry out an evaluation of the system in relation to the Regulation. If non-compliance is found, the authority requires the relevant operator to take appropriate corrective action, withdraw, or recall the system within a reasonable period. Where the operator fails, the authority adopts provisional measures. The Commission and other Member States are informed; objections trigger the Union safeguard procedure (Art 81).

articles.heading: Procedure for Dealing with AI Systems Classified by the Provider as Non-High-Risk in Application of Annex III
articles.summary: Article 80 of the EU AI Act — Procedure for Dealing with AI Systems Classified by the Provider as Non-High-Risk in Application of Annex III. Where a market surveillance authority has sufficient reason to consider that an AI system classified by the provider as not high-risk under Article 6(3) is in fact high-risk, the authority must carry out an evaluation. If the system is found to be high-risk, the authority requires the provider to take all necessary actions to bring it into compliance, including ceasing to use the classification, registering and applying corrective measures. Member States, the Commission and other authorities are informed.

articles.heading: Union Safeguard Procedure
articles.summary: Article 81 of the EU AI Act — Union Safeguard Procedure. Where, within three months of receipt of national notification, objections are raised by other Member States or the Commission against a measure taken under Article 79(5), the Commission must enter into consultation and evaluate the national measure. If considered justified, the Commission's implementing act requires all Member States to ensure the AI system concerned is withdrawn from their market; if not justified, the Member State must withdraw the measure.

articles.heading: Compliant AI Systems Which Present a Risk
articles.summary: Article 82 of the EU AI Act — Compliant AI Systems Which Present a Risk. Where, having performed an Article 79 evaluation, a market surveillance authority finds that, although a high-risk AI system complies with the Regulation, it nevertheless presents a risk to health, safety, fundamental rights, public interest or any other public-policy aspect, the authority requires the operator to take all appropriate measures to ensure the system no longer presents that risk when placed on the market or put into service. Notification to other Member States and the Commission follows.

articles.heading: Formal Non-Compliance
articles.summary: Article 83 of the EU AI Act — Formal Non-Compliance. Where a market surveillance authority makes one of the following findings — CE marking has been affixed in violation of Articles 48 or 49; CE marking has not been affixed; EU declaration of conformity not drawn up or not correctly drawn up; technical documentation unavailable, incomplete or not maintained; registration in the EU database not completed; authorised representative not appointed where required; instructions for use missing — it must require the relevant operator to put an end to the non-compliance within a reasonable period.

articles.heading: Union AI Testing Support Structures
articles.summary: Article 84 of the EU AI Act — Union AI Testing Support Structures. The Commission designates one or more Union AI testing support structures to provide independent technical or scientific advice on request of market surveillance authorities and the Board. Their tasks include evaluations of AI systems, technical analyses for enforcement, and capacity-building. They must operate independently and impartially with adequate funding.

articles.heading: Right to Lodge a Complaint with a Market Surveillance Authority
articles.summary: Article 85 of the EU AI Act — Right to Lodge a Complaint with a Market Surveillance Authority. Without prejudice to other administrative or judicial remedies, any natural or legal person who has grounds to consider that there has been an infringement of the Regulation may submit a complaint to the relevant market surveillance authority. Complaints are handled in accordance with the authority's procedures.

articles.heading: Right to Explanation of Individual Decision-Making
articles.summary: Article 86 of the EU AI Act — Right to Explanation of Individual Decision-Making. Any affected person subject to a decision taken by the deployer on the basis of the output from a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III (except Annex III(2)) that produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects them in a way they consider to adversely impact their health, safety or fundamental rights has the right to obtain from the deployer clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken. Not applicable where Union or national law provides for exceptions or restrictions.

articles.heading: Reporting of Infringements and Protection of Reporting Persons
articles.summary: Article 87 of the EU AI Act — Reporting of Infringements and Protection of Reporting Persons. Directive (EU) 2019/1937 (Whistleblower Directive) applies to the reporting of infringements of this Regulation and the protection of persons reporting such infringements. Encourages internal and external reporting channels and protection against retaliation.

articles.heading: Enforcement of the Obligations of Providers of General-Purpose AI Models
articles.summary: Article 88 of the EU AI Act — Enforcement of the Obligations of Providers of General-Purpose AI Models. The Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V (GPAI obligations under Articles 53–55) on providers of GPAI models, with the AI Office acting on its behalf. National market surveillance authorities maintain general market surveillance over downstream AI systems. The Commission may use the tools in Articles 89–94 — monitoring, requests for documentation, evaluations, requests for measures and procedural rights — to ensure GPAI provider compliance.

articles.heading: Monitoring Actions
articles.summary: Article 89 of the EU AI Act — Monitoring Actions. To carry out the tasks under Section 5, the AI Office may take the necessary actions to monitor effective implementation and compliance with this Regulation by providers of GPAI models, including their adherence to approved codes of practice. Downstream providers have the right to lodge a complaint alleging an infringement and the AI Office's complaint procedure must be duly substantiated.

articles.heading: Alerts of Systemic Risks by the Scientific Panel
articles.summary: Article 90 of the EU AI Act — Alerts of Systemic Risks by the Scientific Panel. The Scientific Panel may provide a qualified alert to the AI Office where it has reason to suspect that a GPAI model poses a concrete identifiable systemic risk at Union level, or that a GPAI model meets the conditions to be classified as having systemic risk. The AI Office takes the alert duly into account when exercising its powers, may request documentation or impose measures, and informs the Board.

articles.heading: Power to Request Documentation and Information
articles.summary: Article 91 of the EU AI Act — Power to Request Documentation and Information. The Commission may request the provider of a GPAI model to provide the documentation drawn up by the provider in accordance with Articles 53 and 55, or any additional information necessary to assess compliance. The request states the legal basis, the purpose, the information required, the time limit and the penalties for non-compliance. Before issuing the request to a non-systemic-risk GPAI provider, the AI Office may initiate a structured dialogue.

articles.heading: Power to Conduct Evaluations
articles.summary: Article 92 of the EU AI Act — Power to Conduct Evaluations. The AI Office, after consulting the Board, may carry out evaluations of the GPAI model concerned in order to assess compliance with the Regulation, in particular where the information obtained under Art 91 is insufficient. Independent experts may be appointed. The provider must provide access including through APIs, source code or other appropriate technical means. Confidentiality applies.

articles.heading: Power to Request Measures
articles.summary: Article 93 of the EU AI Act — Power to Request Measures. Where necessary and appropriate, the Commission may request the GPAI model provider to take appropriate measures to comply with Articles 53 and 55, to implement mitigation measures where an evaluation has raised serious and substantiated concern of a systemic risk at Union level, or to restrict making available, withdraw, or recall the model. The provider may offer commitments to comply, which the Commission may make binding.

articles.heading: Procedural Rights of Economic Operators of the General-Purpose AI Model
articles.summary: Article 94 of the EU AI Act — Procedural Rights of Economic Operators of the General-Purpose AI Model. Article 18 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 applies mutatis mutandis to GPAI model providers, ensuring the right to be heard, the right to access the file, and the right to good administration. Confidentiality protections apply throughout.

articles.heading: Codes of Conduct for Voluntary Application of Specific Requirements
articles.summary: Article 95 of the EU AI Act — Codes of Conduct for Voluntary Application of Specific Requirements. The AI Office and Member States must encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct, including related governance mechanisms, intended to foster the voluntary application to non-high-risk AI systems of some or all of the requirements set out in Chapter III Section 2, taking into account technical solutions and best practices. Also voluntary commitments to additional commitments such as environmental sustainability, AI literacy, inclusive design, diversity, and assessment and prevention of negative impact on vulnerable persons.

articles.heading: Guidelines from the Commission on the Implementation of this Regulation
articles.summary: Article 96 of the EU AI Act — Guidelines from the Commission on the Implementation of this Regulation. The Commission develops guidelines on the practical implementation of the Regulation, in particular on the application of Articles 8–15 and Article 25 (provider obligations), the prohibited practices in Article 5, substantial modification, transparency obligations under Article 50, conditions for high-risk classification under Article 6 (including non-high-risk derogation), and on the relationship between the AI Act and Annex I sectoral law and other relevant Union law including data protection.

articles.heading: Exercise of the Delegation
articles.summary: Article 97 of the EU AI Act — Exercise of the Delegation. The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts under Articles 6(6), 7(1), 7(3), 11(3), 43(5), 43(6), 47(5), 51(3), 52(4) and 53(5) for a period of five years from 1 August 2024 (tacitly extended unless objected). The European Parliament or the Council may object within three months of notification; a delegated act enters into force only if no objection is raised.

articles.heading: Committee Procedure
articles.summary: Article 98 of the EU AI Act — Committee Procedure. The Commission is assisted by a committee within the meaning of Regulation (EU) No 182/2011. Where reference is made to this Article, Article 5 of Regulation (EU) No 182/2011 (examination procedure) applies.

articles.heading: Penalties
articles.summary: Article 99 of the EU AI Act — Penalties. Member States lay down rules on penalties and other enforcement measures, including warnings and non-monetary measures, applicable to infringements of the Regulation by operators, and take all measures necessary to ensure they are properly and effectively implemented. The Regulation itself sets the upper limits: up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover for prohibited-AI breaches (Art 5), up to EUR 15 million or 3% for most other operator breaches, and up to EUR 7.5 million or 1% for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information. SMEs and start-ups face the lower of the percentage or absolute figure.

articles.heading: Administrative Fines on Union Institutions, Bodies, Offices and Agencies
articles.summary: Article 100 of the EU AI Act — Administrative Fines on Union Institutions, Bodies, Offices and Agencies. The European Data Protection Supervisor may impose administrative fines on Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies falling within the scope of the Regulation, up to EUR 1.5 million for non-compliance with prohibited practices and up to EUR 750 000 for non-compliance with other obligations. Mitigating and aggravating circumstances apply.

articles.heading: Fines for Providers of General-Purpose AI Models
articles.summary: Article 101 of the EU AI Act — Fines for Providers of General-Purpose AI Models. The Commission may impose fines on GPAI model providers not exceeding 3% of their total worldwide annual turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 million, whichever is higher, where it finds intentional or negligent infringement of relevant Regulation provisions, failure to comply with documentation or information requests under Art 91, failure to comply with measures requested under Art 93, or failure to make a model available for evaluation under Art 92. Specific criteria guide the amount.

articles.heading: Amendment to Regulation (EC) No 300/2008
articles.summary: Article 102 of the EU AI Act — Amendment to Regulation (EC) No 300/2008. Technical-amendments article: inserts a reference to the AI Act into the civil aviation security framework so that when implementing acts under that Regulation concern AI systems, the AI Act's essential requirements apply. Cross-reference for sectoral integration with Annex I.

articles.heading: Amendment to Regulation (EU) No 167/2013
articles.summary: Article 103 of the EU AI Act — Amendment to Regulation (EU) No 167/2013. Technical-amendments article: inserts a reference to the AI Act into the agricultural and forestry vehicles approval Regulation so AI safety components in these vehicles are subject to AI Act essential requirements. Annex I integration.

articles.heading: Amendment to Regulation (EU) No 168/2013
articles.summary: Article 104 of the EU AI Act — Amendment to Regulation (EU) No 168/2013. Technical-amendments article: inserts a reference to the AI Act into the two- and three-wheel vehicles and quadricycles approval Regulation so AI safety components are subject to AI Act essential requirements. Annex I integration.

articles.heading: Amendment to Directive 2014/90/EU
articles.summary: Article 105 of the EU AI Act — Amendment to Directive 2014/90/EU. Technical-amendments article: inserts a reference to the AI Act into the Marine Equipment Directive so AI safety components in marine equipment are subject to AI Act essential requirements. Annex I integration.

articles.heading: Amendment to Directive (EU) 2016/797
articles.summary: Article 106 of the EU AI Act — Amendment to Directive (EU) 2016/797. Technical-amendments article: inserts a reference to the AI Act into the Interoperability of the Rail System Directive so AI safety components in rail subsystems are subject to AI Act essential requirements. Annex I integration.

articles.heading: Amendment to Regulation (EU) 2018/858
articles.summary: Article 107 of the EU AI Act — Amendment to Regulation (EU) 2018/858. Technical-amendments article: inserts a reference to the AI Act into the type-approval Regulation for motor vehicles and their trailers so AI safety components are subject to AI Act essential requirements. Annex I integration.

articles.heading: Amendments to Regulation (EU) 2018/1139
articles.summary: Article 108 of the EU AI Act — Amendments to Regulation (EU) 2018/1139. Technical-amendments article: inserts a reference to the AI Act into the Civil Aviation Safety Regulation (EASA Basic Regulation) so AI safety components in aviation products are subject to AI Act essential requirements. Annex I integration.

articles.heading: Amendment to Regulation (EU) 2019/2144
articles.summary: Article 109 of the EU AI Act — Amendment to Regulation (EU) 2019/2144. Technical-amendments article: inserts a reference to the AI Act into the General Safety Regulation for motor vehicles so AI safety components in approved vehicles are subject to AI Act essential requirements. Annex I integration.

articles.heading: Amendment to Directive (EU) 2020/1828
articles.summary: Article 110 of the EU AI Act — Amendment to Directive (EU) 2020/1828. Adds the AI Act to Annex I of the Representative Actions Directive, making infringements of the AI Act subject to consumer collective redress brought by qualified entities on behalf of consumers. Significant for class-action style enforcement of AI Act consumer-protection rules.

articles.heading: AI Systems Already Placed on the Market or put into Service and General-Purpose AI Models Already Placed on the Marked [sic]
articles.summary: Article 111 of the EU AI Act — AI Systems Already Placed on the Market or put into Service and General-Purpose AI Models Already Placed on the Market. Transitional regime. AI systems forming components of large-scale IT systems in the area of freedom, security and justice (listed in Annex X) must be brought into compliance by 31 December 2030. Other high-risk systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 are only caught if subsequently subject to significant changes in design. High-risk systems used by public authorities must be in compliance by 2 August 2030. GPAI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 have until 2 August 2027 to comply with Article 53 (and Art 55 where applicable).

articles.heading: Evaluation and Review
articles.summary: Article 112 of the EU AI Act — Evaluation and Review. The Commission must assess the need for amendment of the list of prohibited practices in Article 5, the list of high-risk use cases in Annex III, and the transparency obligations in Article 50, once a year after entry into force and until expiration of the delegation in Article 97. A full evaluation and report to the European Parliament and Council on the application of the Regulation are due by 2 August 2028 and every four years thereafter, addressing financial, human and technical resources, the state of penalty harmonisation, and the operation of the AI Office.

articles.heading: Entry into Force and Application
articles.summary: Article 113 of the EU AI Act — Entry into Force and Application. The Regulation enters into force on the twentieth day following publication (entered into force 1 August 2024). The staggered application schedule: Chapters I (general provisions) and II (prohibited practices, Art 5) apply from 2 February 2025; Chapter III Section 4 (notifying authorities), Chapter V (GPAI), Chapter VII (governance), Chapter XII (penalties) and Articles 78 and 99(7) apply from 2 August 2025 (note: Art 101 fines for GPAI providers apply from 2 August 2026); the bulk of the Regulation including Chapter III high-risk obligations applies from 2 August 2026; and Article 6(1) (Annex I high-risk classification) plus the corresponding obligations apply from 2 August 2027. The master clock.

recitals.summary: Recital 1 of the EU AI Act. States the Regulation's purpose: harmonise the internal market for AI systems while protecting Charter rights, health, safety, democracy, the rule of law and the environment, and preventing Member States from imposing extra restrictions. Foundational framing for every article — read alongside Article 1 (subject matter) and Article 2 (scope) to interpret the balance the Regulation strikes between free movement and rights protection.

Recital 2 of the EU AI Act. Confirms the Regulation must be applied consistently with Union values in the Charter, balancing protection of persons, democracy, the rule of law and the environment against innovation and employment objectives. Useful interpretive anchor when articles trade off rights and innovation (e.g. sandboxes, SME relief, derogations).

Recital 3 of the EU AI Act. Explains the dual Article 114/16 TFEU legal basis: harmonisation across the internal market plus data-protection-driven rules for law-enforcement uses of biometric identification, biometric categorisation, and risk assessments. Justifies consulting the EDPB. Route here when interpreting why Article 5 law-enforcement carve-outs sit alongside product-safety logic.

Recital 4 of the EU AI Act. Catalogues beneficial sectoral uses of AI (healthcare, agriculture, education, energy, transport, environmental monitoring, climate adaptation, etc.) to set up the proportionality argument that follows. Useful when defending non-high-risk classification or when framing socially beneficial use cases under Article 95 codes of conduct.

Recital 5 of the EU AI Act. Notes AI can cause material or immaterial harm — physical, psychological, societal, economic — to public interests and fundamental rights. This is the harm taxonomy that underlies the risk-tiered architecture (prohibited / high-risk / transparency / minimal).

Recital 6 of the EU AI Act. Anchors the Regulation in Article 2 TEU values, Article 6 TEU and the Charter, and states the human-centric principle: AI as a tool serving people. Frequently cited in interpretive disputes about human oversight (Article 14) and the design of trustworthy AI.

Recital 7 of the EU AI Act. Justifies common rules for high-risk AI on Charter, non-discrimination and WTO grounds, and references the AI HLEG Ethics Guidelines and the European Declaration on Digital Rights as soft-law inputs. Route here when arguing about the policy lineage of Articles 8-15 (high-risk requirements).

Recital 8 of the EU AI Act. Restates the case for a harmonised Union framework — free movement, fundamental rights, SME support, ethical principles — citing European Council and Parliament resolutions. Mostly programmatic; useful as a values reference when interpreting innovation-support provisions (Articles 57-63).

Recital 9 of the EU AI Act. Embeds the AI Act in the New Legislative Framework (Regulations 765/2008, 2019/1020 and Decision 768/2008/EC) and clarifies that it is without prejudice to data protection, consumer protection, employment, worker protection, platform work, collective bargaining, and child protection law. Critical interpretive lens when an AI use case sits at the intersection of the AI Act and labour, GDPR, or product-liability regimes.

Recital 10 of the EU AI Act. Confirms the AI Act does not displace GDPR (Regulation 2016/679), the EUDPR (2018/1725), the LED (Directive 2016/680), or ePrivacy (Directive 2002/58/EC). Providers and deployers remain controllers/processors as applicable, and data subjects retain Article 22 GDPR rights on automated decision-making. Essential reference for any GDPR-AI Act overlap analysis.

Recital 11 of the EU AI Act. Carve-out preserving intermediary-service liability rules under the Digital Services Act (Regulation 2022/2065). Cite when scoping platform liability for AI-generated content sitting on hosted services.

Recital 12 of the EU AI Act. Interpretive guide to the Article 3(1) definition of 'AI system': aligned with international (OECD) work, distinguished from deterministic software by the capacity to infer outputs and derive models from inputs. Explains 'machine-based', 'autonomy', 'adaptiveness', 'explicit/implicit objectives', and 'environments'. The primary routing source when arguing whether a specific tool is in or out of scope.

Recital 13 of the EU AI Act. Defines 'deployer' broadly as any natural or legal person, including public authorities, using an AI system under its authority, excluding purely personal non-professional use. Anchors all deployer obligations in Chapter III Section 3 (Articles 26-27).

Recital 14 of the EU AI Act. Aligns 'biometric data' with the GDPR (Article 4(14)), EUDPR (Article 3(18)) and LED (Article 3(13)) definitions. Confirms biometric data can support authentication, identification, categorisation and emotion recognition. Read before applying Articles 5, 26(10) or Annex III(1).

Recital 15 of the EU AI Act. Defines biometric identification as automated recognition (face, gait, voice, keystrokes, etc.) against a reference database, regardless of consent. Excludes one-to-one biometric verification/authentication used solely for service access. Routing source for Article 3(35)-(36) and the Article 5(1)(h) real-time RBI prohibition.

Recital 16 of the EU AI Act. Defines biometric categorisation as assigning persons to categories from biometric data (sex, age, behavioural traits, religion, political orientation, etc.) and creates an exclusion for purely ancillary commercial filters (e.g. marketplace product previews, social-media face filters). Key interpretive source for Article 5(1)(g) and Annex III(1)(b).

Recital 17 of the EU AI Act. Functionally defines 'remote biometric identification system' — identification without the data subject's active involvement, typically at a distance against a reference database — and draws the foundational real-time vs post distinction: real-time covers instant/near-instant live capture; post operates on previously captured material. Essential for routing between Article 5(1)(h) (real-time, prohibited) and Annex III(1)(a) (post, high-risk).

Recital 18 of the EU AI Act. Defines 'emotion recognition system' and lists in/out emotional states. Excludes detection of physical states (pain, fatigue — e.g. driver-drowsiness monitors) and mere detection of expressions/gestures without inferring emotion. Read before applying the Article 5(1)(f) workplace/education prohibition and Annex III(1)(c).

Recital 19 of the EU AI Act. Defines 'publicly accessible space' functionally: any physical space (privately or publicly owned) open to an undetermined number of persons, even when access requires a ticket, registration or age threshold. Excludes online spaces, workplaces, prisons, and border-control areas. Determinative for the geographic scope of the Article 5(1)(h) real-time RBI prohibition and post-RBI use cases in Annex III.

Recital 20 of the EU AI Act. Sets out the AI-literacy concept underlying Article 4: providers, deployers and affected persons must be equipped to understand AI capabilities and impacts. Encourages voluntary codes and tasks the AI Board and Commission with promoting literacy tools.

Recital 21 of the EU AI Act. Establishes non-discriminatory territorial scope: rules apply to providers regardless of EU/third-country establishment and to deployers established in the Union. Read with Article 2 and Recital 22 for extraterritorial reach analysis.

Recital 22 of the EU AI Act. Extends scope to providers and deployers established in third countries when the output of their AI system is intended to be used in the Union — anti-circumvention rule. Carves out third-country public authorities and international organisations acting under law-enforcement/judicial cooperation agreements with adequate safeguards. Foundational for Article 2(1)(c) extraterritoriality analysis.
Recital 23 of the EU AI Act. Brief confirmation that Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies fall in scope when acting as provider or deployer. Cite for any EU-institutional AI use case.

Recital 24 of the EU AI Act. Military, defence and national-security exclusion (Article 2(3)): out of scope regardless of public or private entity. Dual-use systems repurposed for civilian/law-enforcement/humanitarian use fall back in scope, and providers placing systems for mixed civilian-and-defence purposes must comply for the civilian leg. Determinative for many dual-use scoping questions.

Recital 25 of the EU AI Act. Scientific research and development exclusion (Article 2(6)-(8)): AI systems and models developed solely for R&D are out of scope until placed on the market or put into service. Pre-market product-oriented testing is also excluded, without prejudice to sandbox/real-world testing rules. R&D still subject to ethical standards and other Union law.

Recital 26 of the EU AI Act. Articulates the risk-based approach: prohibitions, high-risk requirements, and transparency obligations are tailored to risk intensity. The structural rationale behind Title II (Article 5), Title III, and Article 50.

Recital 27 of the EU AI Act. Recalls the seven non-binding HLEG ethical principles for trustworthy AI — human agency / oversight, robustness and safety, privacy / data governance, transparency, diversity / non-discrimination / fairness, societal and environmental well-being, accountability — and directs that they inform Article 95 codes of conduct. Useful soft-law anchor for design choices around high-risk AI.

Recital 28 of the EU AI Act. Justifies the Article 5 prohibitions on manipulative, exploitative and social-control practices as protecting Charter values: dignity, freedom, equality, non-discrimination, data protection, privacy, and the rights of the child. Framing context for the entire prohibited-practices catalogue.

Recital 29 of the EU AI Act. Detailed interpretation of the Article 5(1)(a) and 5(1)(b) prohibitions on subliminal/manipulative techniques and exploitation of vulnerabilities (age, disability, socioeconomic). Clarifies that intent is not required, distinguishes from common advertising and lawful medical/psychological treatment, and complements the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive. Foundational for any analysis of manipulation-prohibition edge cases.

Recital 30 of the EU AI Act. Explains the Article 5(1)(g) prohibition on biometric categorisation deducing sensitive attributes (political opinions, trade union membership, religion, race, sex life, sexual orientation). Permits lawful labelling/filtering of biometric datasets (e.g. by hair or eye colour) for law-enforcement uses.

Recital 31 of the EU AI Act. Explains the Article 5(1)(c) prohibition on social scoring: AI evaluating natural persons based on social behaviour or personality traits across unrelated contexts, leading to disproportionate detrimental treatment. Does not bar lawful single-purpose evaluations (e.g. credit scoring under sectoral law).

Recital 32 of the EU AI Act. Justifies treating real-time RBI in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement as particularly intrusive (chilling effect on assembly, bias risks by age, ethnicity, race, sex, disability). The threat model behind the Article 5(1)(h) prohibition and its narrow exceptions.

Recital 33 of the EU AI Act. Sets out the exhaustive Article 5(1)(h) carve-out grounds permitting real-time RBI by law enforcement: searching for specific victims (including missing persons), preventing imminent threats to life or terrorist attacks, and locating perpetrators or suspects of the 16 listed serious offences punishable by ≥4 years' custodial sentence (anchored on Framework Decision 2002/584/JHA). Critical companion to Article 5(2)-(6).

Recital 34 of the EU AI Act. Interpretive guidance for Article 5(2): authorities must consider the nature of the situation, proportionality, temporal/geographic/personal scope, complete a fundamental rights impact assessment, and register the system in the EU database. The reference database must fit the use case.

Recital 35 of the EU AI Act. Authorisation regime for real-time RBI under Article 5(3): prior judicial or independent administrative authorisation required, with a narrow 24-hour ex-post urgency exception. Data must be deleted if authorisation is refused. No solely-AI-based adverse legal decisions about a person.

Recital 36 of the EU AI Act. Notification duty: each real-time RBI deployment must be reported to the relevant market surveillance authority and the national DPA, which must annually report aggregated use to the Commission. Operational accountability layer to Article 5(4)-(6).

Recital 37 of the EU AI Act. Member State opt-in: real-time RBI may only be used if expressly authorised in national law. Member States may opt out entirely or restrict authorised grounds, and must notify the Commission of national rules within 30 days. Article 5(5).

Recital 38 of the EU AI Act. Confirms the AI Act's real-time RBI rules are lex specialis to Article 10 LED (Directive 2016/680) for biometric data processing in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement. Non-law-enforcement real-time RBI uses are not covered by this specific authorisation regime.

Recital 39 of the EU AI Act. Reiterates that any biometric identification outside the Article 5 real-time RBI regime stays subject to GDPR Article 9, EUDPR Article 10 and LED Article 10. National DPA prohibition decisions on non-law-enforcement biometric ID remain in force.

Recital 40 of the EU AI Act. Ireland's Protocol No 21 opt-out from specific Article 5 provisions and Article 26(10) to the extent they relate to police and judicial cooperation in criminal matters under Article 16 TFEU. Procedural carve-out, not substantive.

Recital 41 of the EU AI Act. Denmark's parallel Protocol No 22 opt-out from the same Article 5 and Article 26(10) provisions relating to processing of personal data under police and judicial cooperation. Symmetric to Recital 40.

Recital 42 of the EU AI Act. Explains the Article 5(1)(d) prohibition on predictive policing: risk assessments of natural persons based solely on profiling or personality traits to predict criminal offending. Does not bar non-individual risk analytics (e.g. fraud detection on transactions, narcotics-trafficking pattern analysis). Anchored in the presumption of innocence.

Recital 43 of the EU AI Act. Justifies the Article 5(1)(e) prohibition on creating or expanding facial-recognition databases through untargeted scraping of internet images or CCTV footage. Mass-surveillance and privacy rationale.

Recital 44 of the EU AI Act. Scientific basis for the Article 5(1)(f) prohibition on emotion recognition in workplaces and educational institutions: limited reliability, cultural variability, power imbalance, intrusion. Medical and safety uses (e.g. therapeutic systems) are carved out.

Recital 45 of the EU AI Act. Saving clause: practices already prohibited under EU data protection, non-discrimination, consumer protection or competition law remain prohibited regardless of the AI Act. The AI Act does not legitimise otherwise-unlawful processing.

Recital 46 of the EU AI Act. Frames the high-risk regime (Title III): mandatory requirements gate market access. Cross-references the New Legislative Framework, the Blue Guide, and sectoral harmonisation legislation (e.g. Regulations 2017/745 MDR, 2017/746 IVDR, Directive 2006/42/EC Machinery). High-risk classification must minimise restrictions on international trade.

Recital 47 of the EU AI Act. Justifies the high-risk classification of AI safety components of products: autonomous robots in manufacturing/care, sophisticated diagnostics and decision-support in healthcare. Underpins Article 6(1) and Annex I.

Recital 48 of the EU AI Act. Lists the Charter rights relevant to high-risk classification: dignity, private life, data protection, expression, assembly, non-discrimination, education, consumer protection, workers' rights, disability rights, gender equality, IP, effective remedy, fair trial, defence, presumption of innocence, good administration. Highlights children's rights (UNCRC Article 24, General Comment No 25) and the high-level environmental-protection right.

Recital 49 of the EU AI Act. Sectoral safety harmonisation: amends civil aviation security (Regulation 300/2008), agricultural and two/three-wheel vehicle type approval (Regulations 167/2013, 168/2013), marine equipment, rail interoperability, motor-vehicle type approval, civil aviation safety and vehicle general safety to integrate AI Act high-risk requirements without disturbing sectoral conformity assessment governance. Cross-references Article 102-110 amendments.

Recital 50 of the EU AI Act. Article 6(1) classification rule for AI safety components of products: if the product undergoes third-party conformity assessment under listed Union harmonisation law (machinery, toys, lifts, ATEX, radio, pressure, recreational craft, cableways, gas appliances, MDR/IVDR, etc.), the embedded AI system is high-risk. Anchors the Annex I list.

Recital 51 of the EU AI Act. Clarifies that AI-Act high-risk classification does not by itself make the product high-risk under sectoral law — particularly relevant for MDR/IVDR, where third-party conformity assessment applies to medium- and high-risk products alike.

Recital 52 of the EU AI Act. Stand-alone high-risk classification (Article 6(2)): systems in the Annex III pre-defined areas are high-risk where they pose significant harm to health, safety or fundamental rights based on severity and probability. Foundation for the Commission's power to amend Annex III.

Recital 53 of the EU AI Act. Article 6(3) derogation: an Annex III system is not high-risk if it does not materially influence decision-making outcomes — for example, narrow procedural tasks, output review by humans, or tasks improving the result of prior human activity. Always high-risk if it profiles natural persons. Must be documented and registered. Essential for routing borderline Annex III cases.

Recital 54 of the EU AI Act. Justifies high-risk classification of biometric use cases under Annex III(1) — remote biometric identification (post), biometric categorisation by sensitive attributes, and emotion recognition — given technical inaccuracies and discrimination risks. Verification of an individual's claimed identity is excluded from high-risk.

Recital 55 of the EU AI Act. Annex III(2) critical-infrastructure high-risk classification: AI safety components in critical digital infrastructure (NIS2-aligned, Directive 2022/2557), road traffic, and supply of water, gas, heating, electricity. Failure could threaten life, health, and basic supplies.

Recital 56 of the EU AI Act. Annex III(3) education and vocational training high-risk classification: AI for access/admission, assignment to institutions, learning-outcome assessment, level-of-education assessment materially influencing access, and exam-cheating monitoring. Justified by impact on educational paths, livelihoods, and the right to education.

Recital 57 of the EU AI Act. Annex III(4) employment high-risk classification: AI for recruitment, hiring decisions, promotion/termination, task allocation by behaviour or traits, performance monitoring. Covers employees, platform workers and the self-employed. Material impact on career, livelihood and worker rights.

Recital 58 of the EU AI Act. Annex III(5) essential public/private services high-risk classification: eligibility for public assistance, healthcare, social security, social/housing services; credit scoring and creditworthiness (except detection of financial fraud); risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance; emergency dispatch and triage. Heavy reliance and vulnerability rationale.

Recital 59 of the EU AI Act. Annex III(6) law-enforcement high-risk classification: AI for assessing victim risk, polygraphs/emotion inference, evaluating evidence reliability, profiling for re-offending/recidivism (other than the Article 5(1)(d) prohibited category), and profiling during detection/investigation. Power-imbalance and accuracy concerns.

Recital 60 of the EU AI Act. Annex III(7) migration, asylum and border-control high-risk classification: polygraphs, security/health/irregular-migration risk assessments, examination of asylum/visa applications, and detection/identification (excluding travel-document verification). Justified by vulnerability of affected persons.

Recital 61 of the EU AI Act. Annex III(8)(a) justice high-risk classification: AI assisting judicial authorities (or ADR bodies producing legally effective decisions) in researching/interpreting facts and law. Excludes purely administrative ancillary uses (case allocation, anonymisation). Justified by impact on the right to an effective remedy and fair trial.

Recital 62 of the EU AI Act. Annex III(8)(b) democratic-processes high-risk classification: AI intended to influence the outcome of elections/referendums or voting behaviour. Excludes back-office campaign organisation tools to which natural persons are not directly exposed. References Regulation 2024/900 on political advertising.

Recital 63 of the EU AI Act. Saving clause: high-risk classification under the AI Act does not by itself make the use lawful under other Union or national law (data protection, polygraph laws, emotion-detection laws). The AI Act is not a legal basis for personal-data processing.

Recital 64 of the EU AI Act. Introduces the high-risk requirements regime (Articles 8-15): proportionate, state-of-the-art measures tailored to intended purpose and context of use, integrated with the New Legislative Framework. Sets the tone for risk management, data governance, documentation, transparency, oversight, robustness/accuracy/cybersecurity.

Recital 65 of the EU AI Act. Risk-management system (Article 9): continuous, iterative process across the lifecycle to identify and mitigate risks to health, safety and fundamental rights. Must be reviewed and documented; covers known and reasonably foreseeable risks plus residual risk assessment. Applies in addition to existing sectoral risk-management regimes.

Recital 66 of the EU AI Act. Lists the catalogue of high-risk requirements: risk management, data quality, documentation, record-keeping, transparency and deployer information, human oversight, robustness, accuracy and cybersecurity. WTO-compatible (no less trade-restrictive alternatives).

Recital 67 of the EU AI Act. Data governance and data-set quality (Article 10): training/validation/testing data must be relevant, sufficiently representative, free of errors, and complete; labels included. Data-management practices must address bias and discrimination risks. Anchor for any data-quality challenge to a high-risk system.

Recital 68 of the EU AI Act. Encourages access to high-quality datasets via European common data spaces and the AI-on-demand platform for providers, notified bodies, EDIHs, testing facilities and researchers. Public-interest data sharing context for Article 10 implementation.

Recital 69 of the EU AI Act. Privacy by design and data minimisation under GDPR principles apply throughout the AI lifecycle. Permits anonymisation, encryption, federated learning and computation-to-data architectures as compliance techniques.

Recital 70 of the EU AI Act. Article 10(5) carve-out: providers may process Article 9 GDPR special categories where strictly necessary for bias detection and correction in high-risk systems, with technical and organisational safeguards (pseudonymisation, access controls, no further use). Bias-mitigation lawful basis.
