Recital 71 of the EU AI Act. Technical documentation and record-keeping (Articles 11 and 12, Annex IV): essential for traceability, conformity assessment and post-market monitoring. Must cover system characteristics, capabilities, limitations, algorithms, data, training, testing, risk-management. Includes automatic logging.

Recital 72 of the EU AI Act. Transparency to deployers (Article 13): instructions for use must let deployers evaluate functionality, strengths and limitations, including accuracy, robustness, bias risks, foreseeable harms, technical capabilities, intended purpose, training-data characteristics, human-oversight measures, expected lifetime and maintenance.

Recital 73 of the EU AI Act. Human oversight (Article 14): providers must build oversight measures into the system before placement on the market. Human operators must have competence, training and authority; in-built constraints, stop functions and override capabilities; awareness of automation bias; particular safeguards for biometric ID where two-person verification may apply.

Recital 74 of the EU AI Act. Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity (Article 15): consistent lifecycle performance, state-of-the-art benchmarks, transparent metrics in instructions for use, no misleading claims. Aligned with Union legal-metrology law.

Recital 75 of the EU AI Act. Technical robustness (Article 15): resilience against errors, faults, inconsistencies, unexpected situations. Includes fail-safe mechanisms, fallback plans, and addressing feedback loops in adaptive systems.

Recital 76 of the EU AI Act. Cybersecurity (Article 15(5)): resilience against AI-specific attacks — data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples, membership inference, model evasion, confidentiality attacks. State-of-the-art controls expected.

Recital 77 of the EU AI Act. Interface with the Cyber Resilience Act: high-risk AI systems within CRA scope can demonstrate compliance with AI Act cybersecurity requirements by meeting CRA essential cybersecurity requirements. Reduces duplication.

Recital 78 of the EU AI Act. Conformity-assessment alignment with CRA: AI Act procedure applies to CRA essential cybersecurity requirements for high-risk AI products, with a derogation preserving the higher assurance level for CRA critical digital products.

Recital 79 of the EU AI Act. The 'provider' (Article 3(3)) bears responsibility for placing on the market or putting into service a high-risk AI system regardless of whether they designed it. Foundational allocation principle for the Chapter III value-chain rules.

Recital 80 of the EU AI Act. UNCRPD-aligned accessibility: universal-design principles apply to AI systems and services so persons with disabilities have equal access. Connects to the European Accessibility Act (Directive 2019/882) and Web Accessibility Directive (Directive 2016/2102).

Recital 81 of the EU AI Act. Provider quality-management system (Article 17): sound QMS, conformity assessment, technical documentation, robust post-market monitoring. Permits integration with existing sectoral QMS obligations to avoid duplication.

Recital 82 of the EU AI Act. Authorised representative (Article 22): third-country providers must, by written mandate, appoint an EU-established representative who acts as a single point of contact for authorities on compliance, documentation and information requests.

Recital 83 of the EU AI Act. Clarifies roles of importers and distributors in the AI value chain. An operator may hold multiple roles (e.g. distributor and importer) and must cumulatively comply with each.

Recital 84 of the EU AI Act. Re-labelling and substantial-modification rules (Article 25): a distributor, importer, deployer or third party becomes a 'provider' if it puts its name/trademark on a high-risk system, substantially modifies it so it stays high-risk, or modifies the intended purpose to make a non-high-risk system high-risk. Original provider then ceases to be the provider.

Recital 85 of the EU AI Act. General-purpose AI systems may themselves be high-risk or be components of high-risk systems. GPAI providers must closely cooperate with downstream high-risk providers to enable their compliance. Article 25 value-chain cooperation hook.

Recital 86 of the EU AI Act. Where a downstream actor becomes the provider via substantial modification, the original provider must still cooperate by sharing necessary information and technical access for conformity assessment of the modified high-risk system, unless they expressly excluded the modification.

Recital 87 of the EU AI Act. Where a high-risk AI system is a safety component of a product covered by NLF Union harmonisation legislation and is not placed on the market separately, the product manufacturer takes on the AI Act provider obligations to ensure the embedded system complies.

Recital 88 of the EU AI Act. Article 25(4) value-chain cooperation: upstream parties (tool, service, component or process suppliers other than GPAI providers) must, by written agreement, provide downstream providers with necessary information, capabilities and technical access. Commission may publish voluntary model terms.

Recital 89 of the EU AI Act. Free and open-source carve-out from value-chain cooperation obligations for non-GPAI components. FOSS developers are encouraged to publish model cards and data sheets voluntarily. Does not extend to GPAI models or to monetised components.

Recital 90 of the EU AI Act. The Commission may develop voluntary model contractual terms between high-risk providers and upstream suppliers, considering sectoral specificities. Soft-law backstop to Article 25(4).

Recital 91 of the EU AI Act. Deployer obligations (Article 26): technical and organisational measures to use the system per instructions, monitoring functioning, record-keeping, competent and adequately trained oversight personnel. Tailored to deployer-side risks.

Recital 92 of the EU AI Act. Worker information and consultation: deployers must inform workers and their representatives before deploying high-risk AI in the workplace, complementing Directive 2002/14/EC. Ancillary right necessary to protect fundamental rights.

Recital 93 of the EU AI Act. Deployers' role in fundamental-rights protection: best placed to identify context-specific risks not foreseen at design. Specific obligations for non-listed AI uses interacting with workers (impact assessment, training, monitoring).

Recital 94 of the EU AI Act. Biometric identification by law enforcement remains subject to Article 10 LED conditions (strict necessity, safeguards, Union or Member State law basis) and LED Article 4(1) principles (lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, accuracy, storage limitation).

Recital 95 of the EU AI Act. Post-remote biometric identification in law enforcement (Article 26(10)): proportionate, legitimate and strictly necessary, targeted, closed dataset of legally acquired footage. Subject to prior judicial/independent administrative authorisation linked to a specific criminal offence and a suspect. Annual reporting obligation.

Recital 96 of the EU AI Act. Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (Article 27): public bodies, private entities providing public services, and certain Annex III deployers (banking, insurance) must conduct an FRIA before first use of a high-risk system. Covers affected persons, harms, oversight measures, complaints mechanisms.

Recital 97 of the EU AI Act. Defines 'general-purpose AI model' (Article 3(63)) by functional characteristics: generality and competence at a wide range of distinct tasks, typically trained on large datasets via self-supervised, unsupervised or reinforcement learning. Distinguishes GPAI models (component-level) from GPAI systems (Article 3(66)).

Recital 98 of the EU AI Act. Indicative generality threshold: GPAI models with at least one billion parameters trained on large datasets using self-supervision at scale display significant generality. Quantitative anchor for the Article 3(63) definition.

Recital 99 of the EU AI Act. Large generative AI models — text, audio, image, video — are the typical example of GPAI models, accommodating a wide range of distinct tasks. Routing context for ChatGPT/Claude/Gemini-style models.

Recital 100 of the EU AI Act. Integration rule: when a GPAI model is integrated into or forms part of an AI system that can serve a variety of purposes, the result is a 'general-purpose AI system' under Article 3(66). May be used directly or as a component of further systems.

Recital 101 of the EU AI Act. Transparency obligations for GPAI providers (Article 53): keep up-to-date technical documentation for the AI Office and competent authorities, and provide downstream-provider-facing documentation on capabilities and limitations. Proportionality and trade-secret protection apply.

Recital 102 of the EU AI Act. Free and open-source GPAI definition: models whose parameters (including weights), architecture and usage information are publicly available under a licence allowing access, use, modification and redistribution. Excludes models where only model use or distribution-restricted licences apply.

Recital 103 of the EU AI Act. Defines 'free and open-source AI components' broadly (software, data, models, GPAI models, tools, services, processes). Excludes components monetised through paid technical support, paid software-platform access, or use of personal data beyond security/compatibility purposes.

Recital 104 of the EU AI Act. Article 53(2) exemption: FOSS GPAI providers are exempt from the GPAI transparency obligations (technical documentation and downstream-provider documentation) unless the model presents systemic risk under Article 51 — in which case openness is not a defence.

Recital 105 of the EU AI Act. Copyright obligation (Article 53(1)(c)): GPAI providers must put in place a policy to comply with Union copyright law, including respecting Article 4(3) DSM Directive (2019/790) text-and-data-mining opt-outs. Applies regardless of where training takes place. Anchors the central GPAI training-data copyright question.

Recital 106 of the EU AI Act. Reinforces extraterritorial reach of the Article 53(1)(c) copyright-policy obligation: providers placing GPAI models on the Union market comply regardless of where copyright-relevant training activities occur. Anti-circumvention rule for training-data jurisdictions.

Recital 107 of the EU AI Act. Article 53(1)(d) training-data transparency: GPAI providers must publish a sufficiently detailed summary of content used for training using an AI Office template. Comprehensive in scope rather than technically detailed; balances trade-secret protection with rightsholder enforcement.

Recital 108 of the EU AI Act. AI Office role in monitoring copyright-policy and training-data-summary obligations: monitors compliance without work-by-work assessment of training data. Does not affect underlying copyright enforcement.

Recital 109 of the EU AI Act. Proportionality for GPAI compliance: non-professional or scientific-research developers are excluded but encouraged to comply voluntarily. SME/start-up simplified compliance. Substantial modifications/fine-tuning may trigger reclassification; original provider obligations may be limited where the modifier becomes responsible.

Recital 110 of the EU AI Act. Defines 'systemic risk' (Article 3(65)) categories for GPAI: major accidents; disruption of critical sectors; serious public-health-and-safety consequences; harm to democratic processes, public and economic security; dissemination of illegal, false or discriminatory content; CBRN, cyberattack and offensive-cyber risks; loss of human oversight. Capabilities-and-reach driven, lifecycle-wide.

Recital 111 of the EU AI Act. Article 51 classification methodology: a GPAI model has systemic risk if it has high-impact capabilities (matching or exceeding the most advanced models) evaluated via state-of-the-art tools, or significant internal-market impact via reach. Capabilities may be better understood after market release; flexible designation power.

Recital 112 of the EU AI Act. Article 52 classification procedure: provider must notify the AI Office within two weeks of meeting (or knowing it will meet) the systemic-risk threshold, particularly the floating-point-operations (10^25 FLOP) presumption. Provider may rebut the presumption with arguments showing exceptional circumstances. Commission decision binding.

Recital 113 of the EU AI Act. Commission empowered to designate previously-undisclosed GPAI models as having systemic risk, supported by qualified alerts from the scientific panel under Article 90. Closes notification-gap loophole.

Recital 114 of the EU AI Act. Additional obligations for GPAI models with systemic risk (Article 55): model evaluations including adversarial testing; systemic-risk assessment and mitigation; serious-incident tracking and reporting; cybersecurity protection. Applies whether standalone or embedded.

Recital 115 of the EU AI Act. Article 55 incident-reporting duty: serious incidents (and any corrective steps taken) must be reported without undue delay to the Commission and to the relevant national authorities. Providers must also maintain adequate cybersecurity for the model and supporting infrastructure throughout the lifecycle.

Recital 116 of the EU AI Act. Codes of practice (Article 56) — central tool for GPAI compliance, drawn up under AI Office facilitation with national authorities, civil society and the scientific panel. Cover obligations for all GPAI providers and additional ones for systemic-risk providers, including detailed risk taxonomy.

Recital 117 of the EU AI Act. Codes of practice as a presumption of conformity: providers may rely on adopted codes to demonstrate compliance. Commission may approve a code via implementing act with Union-wide validity, or set common implementation rules if a code is not finalised by application date. Eventually displaced by harmonised standards.

Recital 118 of the EU AI Act. Interface with DSA (Regulation 2022/2065) for AI systems embedded in VLOPs/VLOSEs: DSA risk-management framework applies. AI Act obligations are presumed fulfilled to the extent already covered by DSA Article 34/35 risk assessment and mitigation. Avoids duplicative regulation.

Recital 119 of the EU AI Act. Technology-neutral interpretation of DSA intermediary-service definitions: AI systems (e.g. online-chatbot search engines) may be 'online search engines' under the DSA. Coordinates the two regulatory regimes.

Recital 120 of the EU AI Act. Article 50 transparency obligations on synthetic/manipulated content support DSA implementation by VLOPs/VLOSEs in mitigating systemic risks from artificially generated content affecting democratic processes, civic discourse and elections.

Recital 121 of the EU AI Act. Harmonised standards under Regulation 1025/2012 provide the primary route to demonstrate conformity, normally reflecting state of the art. Stakeholder-balanced standardisation (SMEs, consumer organisations, environmental groups, social partners) is encouraged.

Recital 122 of the EU AI Act. Article 40 presumptions: high-risk systems trained and tested on data reflecting the intended geographical, behavioural, contextual or functional setting are presumed to meet data-governance requirements. Cybersecurity certifications under Regulation 2019/881 may presume cybersecurity-requirement compliance.
Recital 123 of the EU AI Act. High-risk AI systems must undergo conformity assessment prior to placing on the market or putting into service (Articles 43-44). Foundational placement-gate rule.

Recital 124 of the EU AI Act. To minimise burden, conformity assessment for high-risk systems embedded in NLF-covered products integrates with existing sectoral assessment procedures. AI Act requirements added without disturbing sectoral methodology.

Recital 125 of the EU AI Act. Conformity-assessment routes for stand-alone Annex III high-risk systems: internal control by default, with third-party (notified body) assessment limited to certain biometric use cases under Annex III(1) — reflecting current pre-market-certification experience.

Recital 126 of the EU AI Act. Notified bodies (Article 29ff): national competent authorities notify them subject to independence, competence, conflict-of-interest and cybersecurity requirements. Notification via the Commission's electronic notification tool under Decision 768/2008/EC Annex I Article R23.

Recital 127 of the EU AI Act. WTO TBT-aligned mutual recognition of conformity-assessment results from third-country bodies meeting AI Act requirements, where the Union has concluded a mutual-recognition agreement. Commission to pursue such agreements actively.

Recital 128 of the EU AI Act. Substantial modification (Article 43(4)): changes to a high-risk system that affect compliance, or changes to intended purpose, trigger a new conformity assessment. Predetermined changes documented in the technical documentation by the original provider do not count as substantial modifications, accommodating systems that 'learn' after deployment.

Recital 129 of the EU AI Act. CE marking (Article 48): high-risk AI systems bear CE marking — physical when embedded in a physical product (optionally complemented by digital), digital-only for digital-only systems. Member States must not create unjustified obstacles to placement.

Recital 130 of the EU AI Act. Article 46 derogation: market surveillance authorities may authorise placement or putting into service without conformity assessment for exceptional public-security, health, environmental or critical-asset reasons. Law-enforcement and civil-protection authorities may also use systems urgently. Conformity assessment must follow promptly.

Recital 131 of the EU AI Act. EU database (Article 71) for high-risk AI systems and providers: registration before market placement, including for Annex III systems where providers claim Article 6(3) non-high-risk derogation. Public-facing for transparency.

Recital 132 of the EU AI Act. Article 50 transparency obligations for AI systems interacting with natural persons or generating content: users must be informed they are interacting with an AI, unless obvious. Carved exceptions for law enforcement under detection/investigation. Applies independently of high-risk classification.

Recital 133 of the EU AI Act. Article 50(2) machine-readable marking obligation: providers of AI systems generating synthetic content (text, audio, image, video) must embed solutions enabling detection that the output is artificially generated/manipulated. Combats misinformation, fraud, impersonation. Excludes assistive editing tools that do not substantially alter input.

Recital 134 of the EU AI Act. Article 50(4) deepfake disclosure: deployers using AI to generate or manipulate image/audio/video content appreciably resembling real persons, objects, places or events ('deep fakes') must disclose artificial origin. Carve-outs for artistic, satirical, fictional or analogous works (limited to disclosure not affecting display) and law-enforcement uses.

Recital 135 of the EU AI Act. Commission may facilitate Union-level codes of practice on detection and labelling of AI-generated content, including detection-mechanism accessibility and provenance verification cooperation across the value chain.

Recital 136 of the EU AI Act. Synthetic-content disclosure obligations support DSA enforcement against VLOPs/VLOSEs disseminating manipulated content affecting democratic processes, civic discourse, electoral processes, illegal content, and public-health/safety risks.

Recital 137 of the EU AI Act. Saving clause: transparency-obligation compliance does not legitimise an otherwise-unlawful AI use under Union/national law, and is without prejudice to other deployer transparency duties.

Recital 138 of the EU AI Act. AI regulatory sandboxes (Article 57): Member States must establish at least one national sandbox by 2 August 2026 for controlled experimentation under regulatory oversight. Joint sandboxes among Member States permitted. Innovation-supporting mechanism.

Recital 139 of the EU AI Act. Sandbox objectives: foster AI innovation, enhance legal certainty, support regulatory learning, facilitate cooperation, accelerate market access, and contribute to evidence-based policy. Bridges between providers and regulators.

Recital 140 of the EU AI Act. Article 59 legal basis for further-processing of personal data within sandboxes for developing public-interest AI systems, under GDPR Article 6(4)/9(2)(g) and parallel EUDPR/LED provisions. All other GDPR obligations and data-subject rights remain applicable. Public-health, environmental, energy, transport, public-administration use cases.

Recital 141 of the EU AI Act. Article 60 real-world testing regime for Annex III high-risk systems outside sandboxes: informed consent of test subjects, market-surveillance-authority registration, plan approval, oversight, withdrawal rights, complaint mechanisms. Strict safeguards to balance innovation against subject impact.

Recital 142 of the EU AI Act. Member States encouraged to support AI R&D promoting socially and environmentally beneficial outcomes (accessibility, equality, environmental targets) through public and Union funding, interdisciplinary cooperation, and stakeholder engagement including ethics commissions.

Recital 143 of the EU AI Act. SME and start-up support: priority access to sandboxes, awareness-raising, dedicated information channels, communication of obligations. Member States must develop targeted initiatives. Foundation for Article 62.
Recital 144 of the EU AI Act. AI-on-demand platform, Digital Europe Programme, Horizon Europe and similar Union funding programmes should support AI Act objectives. Programmatic anchor.

Recital 145 of the EU AI Act. AI-on-demand platform, European Digital Innovation Hubs and testing-and-experimentation facilities support implementation, particularly for SMEs, start-ups and notified bodies. Provide technical and scientific assistance.

Recital 146 of the EU AI Act. Article 63 simplified QMS compliance for microenterprises (€2m turnover, <10 staff): reduces administrative burden without lowering substantive protection. Commission to issue simplified-QMS guidelines.

Recital 147 of the EU AI Act. Commission to facilitate access to testing and experimentation facilities for bodies accredited under Union harmonisation legislation, particularly MDR/IVDR expert panels and reference laboratories.

Recital 148 of the EU AI Act. Governance framework overview (Title VII): coordinates Member State application and Union-level capacity. AI Office established by Commission Decision develops expertise and contributes to Union AI law implementation. Member States facilitate AI Office tasks.

Recital 149 of the EU AI Act. European Artificial Intelligence Board (Article 65): Member State representatives, advisory tasks (opinions, recommendations, guidance), coordination on enforcement, technical specifications and standards, exchange of best practices. Subgroups for market surveillance and notifying authorities.

Recital 150 of the EU AI Act. Advisory forum (Article 67): stakeholder body advising the Board and Commission — industry, start-ups, SMEs, academia, civil society, social partners, Fundamental Rights Agency, ENISA, CEN, CENELEC, ETSI. Balanced commercial and non-commercial representation.

Recital 151 of the EU AI Act. Scientific panel of independent experts (Article 68): supports the AI Office on GPAI monitoring, providing qualified alerts on systemic risks or non-disclosed systemic-risk models. Member States may request panel support for national enforcement against fees covering costs.

Recital 152 of the EU AI Act. Union AI testing support structures: established to provide technical and scientific advice to Member States on enforcement, including testing facilities to be made available to Member States.

Recital 153 of the EU AI Act. Article 70 national competent authorities: each Member State designates at least one notifying authority and one market surveillance authority. Public entities may be appointed. Single point of contact for cross-Member-State coordination encouraged.
Recital 154 of the EU AI Act. National competent authorities exercise powers independently, impartially and without bias. Members subject to confidentiality rules.

Recital 155 of the EU AI Act. Post-market monitoring (Article 72): all high-risk providers must operate a post-market monitoring system tracking real-world performance, interactions with other AI systems, and learning-system risk evolution. Excludes sensitive law-enforcement operational data.

Recital 156 of the EU AI Act. Market surveillance under Regulation 2019/1020 applies in its entirety to AI Act enforcement. Market surveillance authorities have full enforcement powers, exercise them independently, and may also act on non-high-risk systems where risks emerge.

Recital 157 of the EU AI Act. Saving clause for national fundamental-rights authorities: equality bodies, DPAs and similar authorities retain their mandates and may access AI Act documentation where necessary. Article 79 safeguard procedure for systems presenting unacceptable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights.

Recital 158 of the EU AI Act. Financial-services interface: existing internal-governance and risk-management rules in CRR (Regulation 575/2013), CCD (Directive 2008/48/EC), Solvency II (Directive 2009/138/EC), CRD IV (Directive 2013/36/EU), IDD (Directive 2016/97/EU), and MCD (Directive 2014/17/EU) apply alongside the AI Act. Financial supervisors are designated market surveillance authorities for regulated AI uses; AI Act QMS, post-market monitoring and incident reporting integrate with sectoral risk-management. Critical for any bank/insurer high-risk AI analysis.

Recital 159 of the EU AI Act. Specialised market surveillance powers for high-risk biometric AI under Annex III(1) used in law enforcement, migration/asylum/border control, and justice/democracy: investigative and corrective powers including access to all personal data, exercised with complete independence. EDPS supervises Union institutions.

Recital 160 of the EU AI Act. Joint cross-border activities (Regulation 2019/1020 Article 9): market surveillance authorities and the Commission may run joint investigations on high-risk systems presenting serious risk across two or more Member States. AI Office coordinates.

Recital 161 of the EU AI Act. Supervision of AI systems built on GPAI models: where the model and integrating system come from the same provider, AI Office supervises at Union level as market surveillance authority; otherwise national market surveillance authorities supervise the system while AI Office supervises the model.

Recital 162 of the EU AI Act. Commission/AI Office holds exclusive supervisory and enforcement competence for GPAI model provider obligations (Article 88). AI Office may investigate on its own initiative or upon request from market surveillance authorities, supported by the scientific panel.

Recital 163 of the EU AI Act. Scientific panel qualified alerts: support AI Office monitoring by flagging concrete identifiable Union-level risks or potential systemic-risk classification. Article 90 mechanism complementing AI Office monitoring.

Recital 164 of the EU AI Act. AI Office investigative tools (Article 91-92): documentation and information requests, evaluations (including via independent experts), and corrective-measure requests. Code-of-practice compliance is one route to demonstrating GPAI compliance.

Recital 165 of the EU AI Act. Article 95 voluntary codes of conduct: encouraged for non-high-risk AI providers to extend high-risk-style requirements (proportionate to risk and intended purpose), drawing on model and data cards.
Recital 166 of the EU AI Act. Safety-net role of Regulation 2023/988 (General Product Safety Regulation) for non-high-risk AI products. Provides residual product-safety coverage.

Recital 167 of the EU AI Act. Confidentiality duties: authorities must protect IP, confidential business information, trade secrets, public/national security interests, integrity of criminal/administrative proceedings, and classified information in carrying out their tasks.

Recital 168 of the EU AI Act. Penalties (Article 99-101): Member States must lay down effective, proportionate, dissuasive penalties respecting ne bis in idem. Upper limits for fines set at Union level for specific infringements. Article 99 covers prohibited-practices (up to €35m or 7% global turnover), other obligations (up to €15m or 3%), and information provision (up to €7.5m or 1%).

Recital 169 of the EU AI Act. GPAI provider fines (Article 101): up to €15m or 3% of global annual turnover for non-compliance, including failure to follow Commission measures. Limitation periods apply; CJEU has unlimited jurisdiction.

Recital 170 of the EU AI Act. Right to lodge a complaint (Article 85): any natural or legal person with grounds to suspect infringement may complain to the relevant market surveillance authority. Without prejudice to other remedies.

Recital 171 of the EU AI Act. Article 86 right to explanation: affected persons subject to a deployer decision based mainly on output from certain high-risk AI systems, producing legal effects or similarly significant adverse impacts, have a right to a clear and meaningful explanation. Subject to other Union/national law exceptions.
Recital 172 of the EU AI Act. Whistleblower protection: Directive 2019/1937 applies to reporting infringements of the AI Act and protecting reporters.

Recital 173 of the EU AI Act. Article 290 TFEU delegations to the Commission: amending non-high-risk-derogation conditions, the Annex III high-risk list, technical-documentation provisions, declaration-of-conformity content, conformity-assessment procedures, third-party-assessment scope, GPAI systemic-risk thresholds and benchmarks, and Annex XI/XII GPAI documentation requirements.

Recital 174 of the EU AI Act. Review clauses: Commission evaluates and reviews the Regulation by 2 August 2029 and every four years thereafter. Annual assessment of need to amend Annex III and the prohibited-practices list. By 2 August 2028 and every four years, review of GPAI provisions, voluntary requirement uptake, AI Office resourcing, and penalties.
Recital 175 of the EU AI Act. Implementing powers conferred on the Commission under Regulation 182/2011 (comitology) for uniform implementation conditions.

Recital 176 of the EU AI Act. Subsidiarity and proportionality justification: harmonised AI rules cannot be sufficiently achieved by Member States alone and are better achieved at Union level under Article 5 TEU.

Recital 177 of the EU AI Act. Transitional rule for legacy high-risk systems placed on the market or put into service before the general application date: the Regulation applies only if such systems undergo significant changes (equivalent to substantial modification) thereafter. Avoids disruption to existing deployments.
Recital 178 of the EU AI Act. Voluntary early compliance: high-risk providers encouraged to comply with the relevant obligations during the transitional period before the general application date.

Recital 179 of the EU AI Act. Phased application calendar (Article 113): general application 2 August 2026; prohibitions and general provisions from 2 February 2025; GPAI obligations from 2 August 2025; specific high-risk regimes for Annex II-listed product safety-component systems from 2 August 2027. Governance and conformity-assessment infrastructure must be operational by 2 August 2026.

Recital 180 of the EU AI Act. Records the EDPS and EDPB joint consultation under Article 42(1)-(2) EUDPR (Regulation 2018/1725); their joint opinion was delivered on 18 June 2021. Procedural completeness note.

annexes.label: III
annexes.heading: High-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2)
annexes.summary: Annex III enumerates the AI use cases that the Regulation classifies as high-risk under Article 6(2). Listed systems are subject to the full Chapter III Section 2 regime: risk management (Art 9), data governance (Art 10), technical documentation (Art 11), record-keeping (Art 12), transparency to deployers (Art 13), human oversight (Art 14), accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity (Art 15), and the provider/deployer split in Articles 16, 26 and 27. Providers run a conformity assessment, draw up an EU declaration, affix the CE marking, register the system in the EU database, and run post-market monitoring. Annex III becomes generally applicable from 2 August 2026. The Commission may amend the list under Article 7; this snapshot reflects the original adoption text.

items.heading: Biometrics
items.summary: Category 1 — Biometrics. Covers AI that identifies natural persons remotely, categorises them by sensitive or protected attributes, or recognises their emotional state, where Union or Member State law permits the use. Sub-items 1(a)–(c) carve out the specific high-risk subtypes. Many adjacent practices are outright prohibited under Article 5 (e.g. emotion recognition at work and in education, biometric categorisation by race or political opinion). SME-relevant deployment scenarios include identity verification at venues, time-and-attendance systems, and customer analytics — many of which fall outside Annex III if scoped to one-to-one verification (see 1(a) carve-out).

items.label: 1(a)
items.summary: Annex III 1(a) — Remote biometric identification systems. Compare a person's biometric data against a reference database (e.g. CCTV-fed face matching) to identify them without active cooperation. Explicitly excludes one-to-one verification used solely to confirm a person is who they claim to be (e.g. phone-unlock face ID, bank login fingerprint) — this carve-out is the most common SME-relevant boundary. Risk concern: large-scale surveillance, false positives in public spaces. Provider obligations include data governance for the reference dataset (Art 10), accuracy/robustness/bias evaluation (Art 15), human-oversight design (Art 14), and CE marking before placing on the market. Deployers must run a fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 and register the system in the EU database (Art 49(8)).

items.label: 1(b)
items.summary: Annex III 1(b) — Biometric categorisation by sensitive or protected attributes. AI that infers attributes such as religion, political opinion, trade-union membership, sex life, or sexual orientation from biometric data. Distinct from the Article 5 prohibition (which bans inferring race, political opinion, trade-union membership, religious beliefs, sex life, or sexual orientation outright in many contexts) — this Annex III entry covers categorisation by other sensitive attributes that remain permissible under Article 5. Risk concern: discriminatory targeting, profiling drift into prohibited attributes. Triggers full Chapter III Section 2 obligations plus a deployer FRIA (Art 27) given the protected-attribute exposure.

items.label: 1(c)
items.summary: Annex III 1(c) — Emotion recognition systems. AI that infers a person's emotional state from biometric data — facial expression, voice tone, posture. Article 5(1)(f) prohibits use in workplaces and educational institutions except for safety or medical reasons; Annex III 1(c) covers the remaining permissible deployments (retail analytics, security screening, market research). Risk concern: contested scientific validity, false inferences with material consequences, lack of transparency to subjects. Providers and deployers face the full high-risk regime; deployers must inform exposed natural persons under Article 50(3) regardless of any high-risk classification.

items.heading: Critical infrastructure
items.summary: Annex III 2 — Critical infrastructure. AI used as a safety component in the management or operation of critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, or the supply of water, gas, heating, or electricity. The 'safety component' framing is narrower than general use — AI assisting administrative functions of utility companies is not in scope unless its failure would compromise physical safety. Risk concern: cascading failures from AI-driven control of safety-critical systems. Triggers Article 9 risk management with particular emphasis on cybersecurity (Art 15(4)) and human oversight (Art 14). NIS 2 and sector-specific safety regimes apply in parallel.

items.heading: Education and vocational training
items.summary: Category 3 — Education and vocational training. Covers AI used to determine access or admission (3(a)), evaluate learning outcomes (3(b)), assess appropriate education level (3(c)), and monitor for prohibited behaviour during tests (3(d)). Common SME-relevant systems include automated proctoring tools, admission scoring, and adaptive-learning platforms that influence progression. Risk concern: lifelong opportunity foreclosure from automated decisions on educational access. Article 5(1)(f) prohibits emotion recognition in educational settings — a 'stress detection' feature can flip a proctoring tool from Annex III high-risk to outright prohibited.

items.label: 3(a)
items.summary: Annex III 3(a) — Access or admission. AI determining whether natural persons gain access to or are assigned to educational and vocational training institutions at all levels. Risk concern: opaque or biased gating of educational opportunity. Common in university admissions, scholarship allocation, and corporate training tracks. Deployer FRIA under Article 27 effectively mandatory given protected-group exposure. Article 14 human oversight must allow review/override of individual decisions; Article 13 transparency requires the affected applicant know an AI was involved in the decision.

items.label: 3(b)
items.summary: Annex III 3(b) — Evaluate learning outcomes, including AI-driven assessments used to steer the learning process. Covers automated grading, formative-assessment engines, and adaptive-learning platforms whose outputs route students through different content tracks. Risk concern: compounding bias in early-stage assessments that shape later opportunities. Particularly sensitive where outcomes feed admission, certification, or eligibility decisions covered by 3(a) and 3(c). Article 10 data governance must address representativeness of training data across student populations.

items.label: 3(c)
items.summary: Annex III 3(c) — Assess the appropriate level of education an individual will receive or be able to access. Covers placement systems, tracking algorithms, and AI tools that recommend a curricular path or qualification. Risk concern: locking learners into low-opportunity tracks based on early or limited data. Deployer FRIA under Article 27; Article 14 oversight must allow human override of placement decisions; Article 13 transparency obligations to learners and (where applicable) parents or guardians.

items.label: 3(d)
items.summary: Annex III 3(d) — Monitoring and detecting prohibited behaviour of students during tests. Online proctoring, plagiarism detection used during exams, AI-driven invigilation tools. Risk concern: false positives with disciplinary consequences, intrusive monitoring (eye-tracking, room scans). Note: Article 5(1)(f) bars emotion recognition in education — a 'stress detection' feature can flip a proctoring tool from Annex III high-risk to outright prohibited. Deployers must give clear advance notice under Article 13/50 to affected students.

items.heading: Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment
items.summary: Category 4 — Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment. Covers AI used for recruitment/selection (4(a)) and for decisions affecting terms, promotion, termination, task allocation, or performance monitoring (4(b)). SME-critical: any HR-tech tool from CV screening to algorithmic scheduling potentially in scope. Risk concern: opaque adverse decisions on livelihood. Article 5(1)(f) prohibits emotion recognition at work — a workforce-analytics tool that scores employee 'engagement' from camera input is prohibited, not just high-risk. Worker-information obligations under Article 26(7) require deployers to inform workers before deployment.

items.label: 4(a)
items.summary: Annex III 4(a) — Recruitment or selection AI. CV screening, application filtering, candidate scoring, and AI used to place targeted job advertisements (algorithmic targeting that determines who sees a vacancy). Risk concern: discrimination against protected classes amplified by historical hiring data. Deployer FRIA mandatory (Art 27); Article 26(7) requires informing affected workers and worker representatives before deployment; GDPR Article 22 automated-decisions rules also apply where the system makes solely-automated decisions with significant effect.

items.label: 4(b)
items.summary: Annex III 4(b) — Decisions affecting terms of work-related relationships, promotion, termination, task allocation by individual traits, or performance monitoring. Covers algorithmic scheduling, productivity scoring, gig-platform routing, and AI-driven performance reviews. Risk concern: continuous surveillance, opaque adverse outcomes affecting livelihood. Article 26(7) worker-information rights; Article 14 human oversight must allow review of individual decisions; emotion recognition in this context is prohibited under Article 5(1)(f). Trade-union consultation and Member State labour-law obligations apply in parallel.

items.heading: Access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits
items.summary: Category 5 — Access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits. Covers public-benefit eligibility (5(a)), creditworthiness scoring (5(b)), life and health insurance risk pricing (5(c)), and emergency-call triage/dispatch (5(d)). SME-relevant primarily in fintech, insurtech, and healthtech contexts. Risk concern: exclusion from essential services compounding social disadvantage. Deployer FRIA under Article 27 effectively mandatory across this category.

items.label: 5(a)
items.summary: Annex III 5(a) — Public-assistance eligibility AI. Used by public authorities (or those acting on their behalf) to evaluate eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services (including healthcare), and to grant, reduce, revoke, or reclaim such benefits. Risk concern: erroneous benefit cuts to vulnerable populations; the Dutch 'toeslagenaffaire' is the cautionary precedent. Deployer FRIA mandatory; Article 86 right to explanation of individual decisions applies; affected persons can complain to a market surveillance authority under Article 85.

items.label: 5(b)
items.summary: Annex III 5(b) — Creditworthiness evaluation or credit-score generation AI. Covers consumer credit decisions, loan underwriting, and credit-score outputs. Explicit carve-out: AI used solely to detect financial fraud is NOT in this category. Risk concern: opaque credit denial, demographic disparate impact. Particularly SME-relevant for lending fintechs and BNPL operators. Article 86 right to explanation of an individual credit decision applies; GDPR Article 22 also bites where the decision is solely automated. Consumer Credit Directive II overlays additional pre-contractual information duties.

items.label: 5(c)
items.summary: Annex III 5(c) — Risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance. Pricing engines, underwriting AI, and risk classification for life or health policies. General property or motor insurance is NOT in scope. Risk concern: discriminatory pricing on health-state proxies; potential conflict with anti-discrimination law. Solvency II governance obligations apply in parallel; Article 14 human oversight must permit individual underwriting decisions to be reviewed; Article 10 data governance is acute given the protected-attribute exposure (health, genetic data).

items.label: 5(d)
items.summary: Annex III 5(d) — Emergency-call triage and dispatch AI. Evaluates and classifies emergency calls, dispatches or prioritises emergency response (police, fire, medical), and emergency healthcare patient triage. Risk concern: misclassifying urgency leads to life-threatening delays. Article 14 human oversight is the critical control — a dispatcher must remain in the loop. Article 9 risk management must address availability/uptime; Article 15 cybersecurity given the safety-critical role. Medical-device regulation (MDR) may apply in parallel to triage components.

items.heading: Law enforcement
items.summary: Category 6 — Law enforcement. Covers victim-risk assessment (6(a)), polygraph-style tools (6(b)), evidence reliability evaluation (6(c)), individual offending or re-offending risk (6(d)), and profiling during detection/investigation/prosecution (6(e)). Use permitted only where consistent with Union or Member State law. Note: many adjacent uses are prohibited under Article 5 (real-time remote biometric ID in public spaces, predictive policing of individuals based on profiling alone, social scoring). Risk concern: liberty and presumption-of-innocence implications; well-documented historical bias in law-enforcement data.

items.label: 6(a)
items.summary: Annex III 6(a) — Victim-risk AI. Used by or for law enforcement to assess the risk of a natural person becoming the victim of criminal offences (e.g. domestic-violence risk scoring, victim-of-crime probability models). Risk concern: paternalistic or discriminatory targeting of communities flagged as 'at risk'. Deployer FRIA mandatory; Law Enforcement Directive (2016/680) governance applies in parallel; Article 14 oversight must keep individual outreach or intervention decisions human-made.

items.label: 6(b)
items.summary: Annex III 6(b) — Polygraph or similar tools used by or for law enforcement. AI-driven deception detection, voice-stress analysis, or micro-expression scoring used during investigative interviews. Risk concern: scientific reliability of the underlying signals is contested; false positives can materially affect suspects and witnesses. Article 10 data governance must document training-data representativeness; Article 13 transparency obligations to subjects exposed to the system. Some Member States prohibit polygraph evidence outright — local-law check required.

items.label: 6(c)
items.summary: Annex III 6(c) — Evidence reliability evaluation AI. Used by or for law enforcement to assess the reliability of evidence in investigation or prosecution. Includes AI weighing the credibility of forensic outputs or witness statements. Risk concern: opaque influence on prosecutorial decision-making. Article 14 oversight must place a human at the decision point; the Law Enforcement Directive requires the data-protection rights of suspects and other parties to be preserved through any AI-mediated assessment.

items.label: 6(d)
items.summary: Annex III 6(d) — Risk of offending or re-offending assessment AI; or AI assessing personality traits, characteristics, or past criminal behaviour of natural persons or groups. Explicitly excludes systems that rely solely on profiling under LED Article 3(4) — those are governed by Article 5 prohibitions instead. Risk concern: 'COMPAS-style' tools shaping sentencing or supervision decisions, demographic-bias amplification. Deployer FRIA mandatory; Article 86 right to explanation; LED rules on automated decisions apply alongside Article 14 oversight.

items.label: 6(e)
items.summary: Annex III 6(e) — Profiling of natural persons (LED Article 3(4)) by or for law enforcement during detection, investigation, or prosecution of criminal offences. Distinct from 6(d): this is profiling used in active enforcement, not generic risk scoring. Risk concern: disproportionate targeting of demographics, chilling effects on rights of assembly and expression. Article 27 FRIA mandatory; LED transparency rules apply; Article 5(1)(d) prohibits predictive policing based solely on profiling — boundary check required.

items.heading: Migration, asylum and border control management
items.summary: Category 7 — Migration, asylum and border control management. Covers polygraph tools (7(a)), risk assessment of entrants (7(b)), application-examination assistance (7(c)), and identification in the migration context excluding travel-document verification (7(d)). Use permitted only where consistent with Union or Member State law. Risk concern: high-stakes decisions on protection rights, presumed power imbalance, downstream Schengen-database effects. Coverage explicitly excludes AI used solely for travel-document verification — the most common SME-adjacent use case (e.g. e-gate document checks) tends to fall outside Annex III.

items.label: 7(a)
items.summary: Annex III 7(a) — Polygraph or similar tools used by or for competent public authorities in the migration context. Examples: AI-driven credibility scoring of asylum-interview testimony. Risk concern: contested scientific validity used to deny protection rights. Article 10 data governance, Article 13 transparency, Article 14 oversight all critical; the Law Enforcement Directive and asylum-procedures rules apply in parallel.

items.label: 7(b)
items.summary: Annex III 7(b) — Risk-assessment AI for entrants. Assesses security risk, irregular-migration risk, or health risk posed by a person intending to enter or who has entered a Member State. Common deployments: pre-travel screening, automated risk flags at border crossings. Risk concern: opaque adverse decisions affecting fundamental rights; downstream cascade into other systems (visas, residence permits). Article 27 FRIA mandatory; Article 86 right to explanation; Article 14 human oversight must keep entry decisions reviewable.

items.label: 7(c)
items.summary: Annex III 7(c) — AI assisting competent public authorities to examine applications for asylum, visa, or residence permits and associated complaints, including assessments of the reliability of evidence supporting an application. Risk concern: protection-claims decided by AI-influenced scoring, vulnerable applicants. Article 14 oversight must put a human at the decision point; Article 86 right to explanation for the applicant; LED, asylum-procedures, and visa-code obligations apply in parallel.

items.label: 7(d)
items.summary: Annex III 7(d) — Identification of natural persons by competent authorities in the migration, asylum, or border-control context. Excludes the verification of travel documents — the most common e-gate use case is outside Annex III. Risk concern: misidentification leading to wrongful detention or refusal of entry. Article 9 risk management with particular attention to accuracy under field conditions; Article 14 human oversight; Article 13 transparency on accuracy limits to operators.

items.heading: Administration of justice and democratic processes
items.summary: Category 8 — Administration of justice and democratic processes. Covers AI assisting judicial authorities in research and application of law (8(a)) and AI influencing election or referendum outcomes or voting behaviour (8(b)). The 8(b) carve-out for purely administrative or logistical political-campaign tools is important — most SME-relevant civic-tech sits in that excluded zone.

items.label: 8(a)
items.summary: Annex III 8(a) — AI assisting a judicial authority in researching and interpreting facts and the law, applying the law to concrete facts, or used similarly in alternative dispute resolution. Includes legal-research copilots and AI-drafted opinions used internally by judges or arbitrators. Risk concern: erosion of judicial independence, opaque influence on rulings. Article 14 oversight: the AI never decides — the judge does. Article 13 transparency must clarify the AI role to all parties. Note: practitioner tools used by lawyers (not by judges) fall outside this entry.

items.label: 8(b)
items.summary: Annex III 8(b) — AI intended to influence the outcome of an election or referendum or the voting behaviour of natural persons in elections or referenda. Covers micro-targeted political messaging, AI-driven persuasion campaigns aimed at individual voters. Explicit carve-out: AI to which natural persons are NOT directly exposed (campaign analytics, logistics, organisation tools) is OUT of Annex III — most SME civic-tech lives in that excluded zone. Risk concern: information integrity, manipulation of democratic processes. Deployers must run a FRIA (Art 27); Article 50 transparency obligations to exposed voters apply; the Digital Services Act overlays advertising-transparency duties.
